The multiplier is -2 divided by 1, which is -2, so we do R3 -> R3 - (-2) R2, in other words R3 -> R3 + 2 R2. Row 3 becomes [0, -2 + 2, 1 - 2 | -1 - 2] = [0 0 -1 | -3]. The matrix is now [1 1 1 | 6], [0 1 -1 | -1], [0 0 -1 | -3]. That is row echelon form, with pivots 1, 1 and -1 on the staircase.

Back substitution: Read the staircase from the bottom up. The last row says -z = -3, so z = 3. The middle row says y - z = -1, so y = -1 + 3 = 2. The top row says x + y + z = 6, so x = 6 - 2 - 3 = 1. The solution is (x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3). Always check by plugging back in: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, 2 + 6 + 3 = 11 and 1 - 2 + 6 = 5. All three are true, so we are done. This checking step takes ten seconds and saves many lost marks.

When the pivot spot is zero: Suppose the system is 2y = 4 and x + y = 3. The augmented matrix is [0 2 | 4] and [1 1 | 3]. The top-left entry is 0, and you cannot divide by zero to compute a multiplier. The fix is easy: swap the rows, R1 <-> R2, giving [1 1 | 3] and [0 2 | 4]. It is already in echelon form. Back substitution gives y = 2 and x = 1. Whenever a pivot position holds a zero, look down the column for a nonzero entry and swap it up. If the whole rest of the column is zero, that column has no pivot and you move one column to the right.

Spotting no solution: Try x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 5. Do R2 -> R2 - 2 R1 and the second row becomes [0 0 | 1]. Read it as an equation: 0x + 0y = 1, which says 0 = 1. That is impossible, so the system is inconsistent and has no solution. The rule to remember: if elimination ever produces a row of the form [0 0 ... 0 | c] with c not zero, stop. There is no solution. Geometrically, the two lines were parallel.

Spotting infinitely many solutions: Try x + 2y = 3 and 2x + 4y = 6. Do R2 -> R2 - 2 R1 and the second row becomes [0 0 | 0], which just says 0 = 0. That is always true and carries no information. We end up with only one real equation, x + 2y = 3, for two unknowns. The column of y has no pivot, so y can be anything and x = 3 - 2y follows. There are infinitely many solutions. Describing them neatly with free variables is the main job of the next lesson on Gauss-Jordan elimination and RREF.

Counting the cost: For an n by n system, eliminating below the pivots takes roughly (2/3) n^3 arithmetic operations, while back substitution takes only about n^2. So doubling the number of unknowns makes elimination about eight times slower. A 1000 by 1000 system needs on the order of 670 million operations, which a laptop handles in well under a second. That is why elimination, not guessing or substitution, is the workhorse of scientific computing. We will look at this more carefully in the LU lesson.

Real life example 1, the fruit shop in Karwan Bazar: A wholesaler sells mangoes, bananas and lychees by the dozen. Customer A buys 1 dozen of each and pays 6 hundred taka. Customer B buys 2 dozen mangoes, 3 dozen bananas and 1 dozen lychees for 11 hundred taka. Customer C buys 1 dozen mangoes, returns 1 dozen bananas for credit and buys 2 dozen lychees, paying 5 hundred taka. Write m, b and l for the prices in hundreds of taka per dozen and you get exactly our worked example. So m = 1, b = 2 and l = 3, meaning mangoes cost 100, bananas 200 and lychees 300 taka per dozen. The same three steps would work for a shop with 40 products and 40 receipts, just with a computer doing the arithmetic.

Real life example 2, electric circuits: In an EEE lab at BUET or any university, students apply Kirchhoff's laws to a circuit with several loops. Each loop and each junction gives one linear equation in the unknown currents I1, I2, I3 and so on. A circuit with 10 loops gives a 10 by 10 system. Circuit simulators like SPICE build such systems automatically and solve them with elimination-based methods thousands of times per second while simulating how the circuit changes over time. Weather forecasts, bridge designs and game physics engines do the same with systems that have millions of unknowns.

Common mistake 1, forgetting the right side: When you do R2 -> R2 - 2 R1, you must apply it to every entry of the row, including the number after the bar. Students often update the coefficients and forget b. Common mistake 2, using a changed row too early: if you change R1 and then use R1 to fix R3 in the same step, you must use the new R1, and it is easier to just change one row at a time and rewrite the matrix. Common mistake 3, multiplying a row by zero, which is not allowed. Common mistake 4, sign errors with negative multipliers; write R3 -> R3 + 2 R2 instead of R3 -> R3 - (-2) R2 to stay safe.

Another confusion: Row echelon form is not unique. If you choose different pivots or scale rows differently, you can reach different staircases from the same matrix. The solutions you get at the end are the same, and the positions of the pivots are the same, but the numbers inside can differ. Only the reduced row echelon form, which we meet next lesson, is unique. So do not panic if your REF looks different from your friend's; check the final answer instead.

What exams ask: Typical questions are, solve this 3 by 3 system using Gaussian elimination and show every row operation; reduce this matrix to row echelon form and identify the pivots; decide whether the system is consistent. A favourite twist adds a parameter. For example, for which k does x + y = 2, 2x + ky = 5 have a unique solution? Do R2 -> R2 - 2 R1 to get [0, k - 2 | 1]. If k is not 2, the second row has a pivot and there is exactly one solution. If k = 2, the row becomes [0 0 | 1], meaning 0 = 1, so there is no solution. Practice a few of these, they are easy marks once you see the pattern.

Recap: Gaussian elimination solves Ax = b by using three safe row operations (swap, scale by nonzero, add a multiple of another row) to turn the augmented matrix into a staircase called row echelon form. Pivots sit on the corners of the staircase. Back substitution then reads off the unknowns from the bottom up. A row [0 ... 0 | c] with c nonzero means no solution, a column without a pivot means a free variable and infinitely many solutions, and otherwise the solution is unique. Next lesson we keep going past the staircase to the fully cleaned form, RREF.
key_points: Three elementary row operations: swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero number, add a multiple of one row to another.
Row operations never change the solution set, because each one can be undone.
Row echelon form: zero rows at the bottom, each pivot to the right of the one above, zeros below every pivot.
Multiplier m = (entry to eliminate) / (pivot); do Ri -> Ri - m R(pivot row).
If a pivot position is zero, swap with a lower row that has a nonzero entry there.
Back substitution solves the staircase from the last equation upward.
A row [0 ... 0 | c] with c != 0 means no solution; a column with no pivot means infinitely many (if consistent).
Elimination costs about (2/3)n^3 operations for an n x n system.
lessons.tip: Write the row operation (like R3 -> R3 - 2R1) next to every new matrix you draw, and always plug your final answer back into the original equations. Examiners give marks for the steps, and the check catches almost every arithmetic slip.
lessons.task: On paper, solve 2x + y - z = 1, x + y + z = 6, 3x - y + 2z = 7 with Gaussian elimination, writing each row operation next to each matrix. Plug your answer back into all three equations, then verify it with any free online matrix calculator on your phone.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an elementary row operation?
quiz.explain: Multiplying a row by 0 destroys information and cannot be undone, so it is not allowed.

quiz.q: While eliminating, you get the row [0 0 0 | 7]. What does it mean?
quiz.explain: The row says 0 = 7, which is impossible, so the system is inconsistent.

quiz.q: The pivot is 2 and the entry below it is 6. Which operation clears the 6?
quiz.explain: Multiplier m = 6 / 2 = 3, so subtract 3 times the pivot row.

quiz.q: After elimination you have z = 2, y + z = 5, x + y + z = 9. What is x?
quiz.explain: Back substitution: z = 2, y = 3, x = 9 - 3 - 2 = 4.

quiz.q: Roughly how does the work of Gaussian elimination grow for an n x n system?
quiz.explain: Elimination needs about (2/3)n^3 operations, so doubling n makes it about 8 times slower.

lessons.title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and RREF
lessons.content:
Think about tidying a cupboard. Gaussian elimination is like pushing everything to the back shelves so nothing falls out. That is good, but you still have to dig around to find your cricket bat. Gauss-Jordan elimination goes one step further: every item gets its own labelled spot, so you just open the door and read off where everything is. In matrix language, that perfectly labelled cupboard is called the reduced row echelon form, or RREF.

Where we are: In the last lesson we turned a system into a staircase called row echelon form (REF) and then used back substitution. We also saw that some systems have infinitely many solutions, but we did not yet have a clean way to write them down. This lesson fixes that. We will learn the fully reduced form, the difference between pivot variables and free variables, how to write infinitely many solutions in parametric form, and what is special about homogeneous systems where the right side is all zeros.

Reduced row echelon form: A matrix is in RREF when it is in row echelon form and two more rules hold. First, every pivot equals 1 (these are called leading 1s). Second, each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column, so there are zeros both below and above every pivot. For example, the matrix with rows [1 0 0 | 1], [0 1 0 | 2], [0 0 1 | 3] is in RREF, and so is [1 2 0 | 3], [0 0 1 | 1]. But [1 2 3], [0 1 4] is not, because the 2 sits above the second pivot.

Why RREF is special: Row echelon form is not unique; two people can reach different staircases. RREF is unique. Every matrix has exactly one RREF no matter which legal row operations you use or in which order. That makes RREF a fingerprint of the matrix. Computer algebra tools like MATLAB, Octave and SymPy have a function called rref exactly for this reason, and when you and a friend both reduce the same matrix correctly, your RREFs must match exactly.

Gauss-Jordan elimination: The method has two phases. The forward phase is ordinary Gaussian elimination, going left to right and clearing entries below each pivot. The backward phase starts at the rightmost pivot and works upward and leftward: scale each pivot row so the pivot becomes 1, then subtract multiples of it from the rows above to clear the entries above the pivot. When you reach the top left, you are in RREF, and the answer can be read straight off without any back substitution.

A worked example: Last lesson we solved x + y + z = 6, 2x + 3y + z = 11, x - y + 2z = 5 and reached the REF with rows [1 1 1 | 6], [0 1 -1 | -1], [0 0 -1 | -3]. Now the backward phase. Scale the last row by -1: R3 -> -R3 gives [0 0 1 | 3]. Clear above it: R2 -> R2 + R3 gives [0 1 0 | 2], and R1 -> R1 - R3 gives [1 1 0 | 3]. Finally clear above the second pivot: R1 -> R1 - R2 gives [1 0 0 | 1]. The RREF is [1 0 0 | 1], [0 1 0 | 2], [0 0 1 | 3], which literally says x = 1, y = 2, z = 3.

Gauss-Jordan versus Gaussian: For solving one system by hand, Gaussian elimination plus back substitution is slightly less work, about n^3/3 multiplications against about n^3/2 for full Gauss-Jordan. But Gauss-Jordan shines when you want to see the structure of the solution set clearly, and it is the standard method for computing the inverse of a matrix, which is next lesson. So learn both and use whichever the question asks for.

Pivot variables and free variables: Once a system is in RREF, look at which columns contain a pivot. The unknowns belonging to pivot columns are called pivot variables (also leading or basic variables). The unknowns belonging to columns without a pivot are called free variables. Free variables can take any value you like, and each choice decides the pivot variables. The number of free variables equals the number of unknowns minus the number of pivots.

A system with a free variable: Solve x + 2y + z = 4 and 2x + 4y + 3z = 9. The augmented matrix has rows [1 2 1 | 4] and [2 4 3 | 9]. Do R2 -> R2 - 2 R1 to get [0 0 1 | 1]. Notice the second pivot jumps to column 3, because column 2 below the first pivot is already zero. Now clear above it: R1 -> R1 - R2 gives [1 2 0 | 3]. The RREF is [1 2 0 | 3], [0 0 1 | 1]. Pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so x and z are pivot variables and y is free.

Writing the parametric solution: Read each row as an equation and move free variables to the right side. Row 1 says x + 2y = 3, so x = 3 - 2y. Row 2 says z = 1. Now give the free variable a name like t, so y = t. The full solution is x = 3 - 2t, y = t, z = 1, where t is any real number. Try t = 0: (3, 0, 1), and 3 + 0 + 1 = 4, 6 + 0 + 3 = 9. Try t = 1: (1, 1, 1), and 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, 2 + 4 + 3 = 9. Both work, and so does every other t.

Vector form: The same answer can be written as one vector equation: (x, y, z) = (3, 0, 1) + t(-2, 1, 0). This is very readable. The first vector is one particular solution. The second vector is a direction, and adding any multiple of it moves you along a line of solutions. Geometrically, the two planes x + 2y + z = 4 and 2x + 4y + 3z = 9 meet along exactly this line in 3D space. With two free variables you get two direction vectors and a whole plane of solutions, and so on.

Reading the answer from RREF: Here is the complete decision rule. If the RREF has a pivot in the last column (the one after the bar), meaning a row [0 0 ... 0 | 1], the system is inconsistent: no solution. Otherwise the system is consistent. If it is consistent and every variable column has a pivot, there are no free variables and the solution is unique. If it is consistent and at least one variable is free, there are infinitely many solutions. That is the whole story of one, none or infinitely many, now with a clear test.

Rank, first look: The number of pivots in the RREF of A is called the rank of A. With n unknowns, number of free variables = n - rank. For a consistent system, rank = n means a unique solution, and rank less than n means infinitely many. We will meet rank again properly in the lesson on the four fundamental subspaces, along with the rank-nullity theorem, which is really this same counting fact in fancier clothes.

Homogeneous systems: A system is homogeneous when every right-hand side is zero, so it looks like Ax = 0. Such a system is always consistent, because x = 0 (all unknowns zero) always works. That boring answer is called the trivial solution. The interesting question is whether there are nontrivial solutions, meaning solutions where not all unknowns are zero. There are nontrivial solutions exactly when there is at least one free variable.

A homogeneous example: Solve x + y + z = 0 and x - y + 2z = 0. Row reduce: R2 -> R2 - R1 gives [0 -2 1 | 0]. Scale: R2 -> (-1/2) R2 gives [0 1 -1/2 | 0]. Clear above: R1 -> R1 - R2 gives [1 0 3/2 | 0]. So x = -(3/2) z and y = (1/2) z, with z free. Let z = 2s to avoid fractions: (x, y, z) = s(-3, 1, 2). Check s = 1: -3 + 1 + 2 = 0 and -3 - 1 + 4 = 0. The solutions form a line through the origin.

The more-unknowns-than-equations rule: If a homogeneous system has more unknowns than equations, it must have nontrivial solutions. Why? Each row can hold at most one pivot, so with m equations there are at most m pivots. If n is bigger than m, at least n - m columns have no pivot, so there is at least one free variable. Our example had 2 equations and 3 unknowns, so we knew in advance there would be a free variable. This simple fact shows up again and again, for example when proving that too many vectors must be linearly dependent.

Particular plus homogeneous: Look back at the earlier solution (3, 0, 1) + t(-2, 1, 0). Plug the direction (-2, 1, 0) into the left sides: -2 + 2 + 0 = 0 and -4 + 4 + 0 = 0. It solves the homogeneous version Ax = 0. This is always true. Every solution of Ax = b equals one particular solution plus some solution of Ax = 0. A nice way to picture it: the solution set of Ax = b is the solution set of Ax = 0 slid over to pass through one particular point.

Real life example 1, balancing chemical equations: In chemistry class you balance a H2 + b O2 -> c H2O. Counting atoms gives a homogeneous system. Hydrogen: 2a = 2c. Oxygen: 2b = c. Rewrite as 2a - 2c = 0 and 2b - c = 0. Two equations, three unknowns, so there must be a free variable. Take c as free: a = c and b = c/2. The smallest whole numbers come from c = 2, giving a = 2, b = 1: 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O. Any multiple, like 4 H2 + 2 O2 -> 4 H2O, also balances, which is exactly what a free variable predicts.

Real life example 2, the tiffin budget: You have exactly 100 taka and want exactly 12 items from the canteen: singaras at 10 taka, puris at 5 taka and cups of tea at 10 taka. With x singaras, y puris and z teas, the system is x + y + z = 12 and 10x + 5y + 10z = 100. Row reduce: R2 -> R2 - 10 R1 gives [0 -5 0 | -20], so y = 4. Then R1 gives x + z = 8. With z = t free: x = 8 - t, y = 4, z = t. In real life only whole numbers from 0 to 8 make sense for t, so you have 9 possible tiffin plans, like 8 singaras and 4 puris, or 5 singaras, 4 puris and 3 teas.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to make pivots equal to 1, which leaves you in REF and not RREF. Clearing below pivots but forgetting above. Treating the column after the bar as a variable column; it is never a free variable. Picking a pivot variable as the free one, for example writing x = t in the example above, which can work by luck but is not the standard and often gives a messier answer. Sign errors when moving free variables to the right side: from x + 2y = 3 you get x = 3 - 2y, not 3 + 2y. And forgetting to state that t is any real number.

What exams ask: Reduce this matrix to RREF using Gauss-Jordan elimination. Find the general solution of this system in parametric or vector form. Identify the pivot and free variables. Find the rank. Show that a homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution. Decide, for which values of k the system has no solution, a unique solution or infinitely many. And sometimes: show that the solution of Ax = b is a particular solution plus the solution of Ax = 0. All of these use the same skill, so practice reducing a few 3 by 4 matrices until it feels routine.

Recap: RREF is REF with leading 1s and zeros above and below every pivot, and it is unique for each matrix. Gauss-Jordan elimination gets there by a forward phase and a backward phase. Columns with pivots give pivot variables, columns without give free variables, and free variables become parameters like t and s in the general solution. A pivot in the last column means no solution. A homogeneous system Ax = 0 always has the trivial solution, and has nontrivial ones exactly when there is a free variable, which is guaranteed when unknowns outnumber equations. Next up: matrix inverses, where Gauss-Jordan becomes a machine for computing A^-1.
key_points: RREF = REF + every pivot is 1 + each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column.
Every matrix has exactly one RREF, so RREF is like a fingerprint.
Gauss-Jordan: forward phase clears below pivots, backward phase scales pivots to 1 and clears above them.
Pivot columns give pivot variables; columns without pivots give free variables (any value).
General solution in vector form: particular solution + t(direction) + s(direction) ...
Pivot in the last (augmented) column means no solution; consistent with a free variable means infinitely many.
Homogeneous Ax = 0 always has x = 0; it has nontrivial solutions iff there is a free variable.
More unknowns than equations in a homogeneous system guarantees nontrivial solutions.
lessons.tip: After you reach RREF, circle each pivot. Every uncircled variable column is free, give it a letter like t or s, and write each pivot variable in terms of those letters. Then plug in t = 0 and t = 1 to check quickly.
lessons.task: On paper, put the matrix with rows [1 2 -1 | 3] and [2 4 1 | 9] into RREF using Gauss-Jordan elimination. Name the pivot and free variables, write the general solution in vector form, and check it by plugging in two different values of the free variable.

quiz.q: Which matrix is in reduced row echelon form?
quiz.explain: [1 0 4], [0 1 5] has leading 1s with zeros above and below each pivot. The others have a nonzero above a pivot, a pivot that is not 1, or pivots in the wrong order.

quiz.q: The RREF of a system is [1 3 0 | 2], [0 0 1 | 5]. Which variable is free?
quiz.explain: Pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so the column of y has no pivot and y is free.

quiz.q: In the same system [1 3 0 | 2], [0 0 1 | 5], what is the general solution?
quiz.explain: Row 1 gives x + 3y = 2, so x = 2 - 3y; with y = t and z = 5.

quiz.q: A homogeneous system has 3 equations and 5 unknowns. What can you say for sure?
options: It has only the trivial solution
quiz.explain: At most 3 pivots for 5 unknowns leaves at least 2 free variables, so infinitely many (nontrivial) solutions.

quiz.q: Which statement about RREF is true?
options: A matrix can have many different RREFs
RREF requires every entry to be 1
Gaussian and Gauss-Jordan always give the same REF
Every matrix has exactly one RREF
quiz.explain: RREF is unique, unlike REF which depends on the choices you make.

lessons.title: Matrix Inverse
lessons.content:
Imagine you put on your socks and then your shoes. To undo that at night, you take off the shoes first and then the socks. Undoing goes in reverse order. Now think of a matrix as a machine that transforms vectors: it stretches, turns or mixes them. A natural question is whether there is an undo machine that brings every vector back to where it started. When such an undo machine exists, it is called the inverse of the matrix, and this lesson is all about it.

Numbers first: For ordinary numbers, the inverse of 5 is 1/5, because 5 times 1/5 = 1. The number 1 is special because multiplying by it changes nothing. Every nonzero number has an inverse, but 0 does not, since 0 times anything is 0 and never 1. Matrices work the same way, with one twist: many nonzero matrices also have no inverse. Part of this lesson is learning how to tell which ones do.

The definition: Let A be a square n by n matrix. A is called invertible (or nonsingular) if there is an n by n matrix B such that AB = I and BA = I, where I is the identity matrix. Such a B is called the inverse of A and written A^-1. If no such matrix exists, A is called singular or non-invertible. Only square matrices can have a two-sided inverse in this sense. For square matrices, it turns out that checking just one side is enough: if AB = I, then BA = I automatically.

The inverse is unique: Could a matrix have two different inverses? No. Suppose B and C are both inverses of A. Then B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C. So B and C are the same matrix. That is why we can safely say the inverse and use the symbol A^-1. Note that A^-1 is not 1/A, and you never divide by a matrix. You multiply by its inverse, on the correct side.

The 2 by 2 formula: For A = [a b; c d], the number ad - bc is called the determinant of A. If ad - bc is not 0, then A^-1 = (1/(ad - bc)) [d -b; -c a]. In words: swap the two diagonal entries, change the signs of the two off-diagonal entries, and divide everything by ad - bc. If ad - bc = 0, the matrix has no inverse. Determinants get their own two lessons later; for now ad - bc is just the magic number for 2 by 2.

Trying the formula: Take A = [2 1; 1 1]. Then ad - bc = 2 - 1 = 1, so A^-1 = [1 -1; -1 2]. Check: [2 1; 1 1] times [1 -1; -1 2]. Row 1 times column 1 is 2 - 1 = 1, row 1 times column 2 is -2 + 2 = 0, row 2 times column 1 is 1 - 1 = 0, row 2 times column 2 is -1 + 2 = 1. We get I, so it works. Now take B = [1 2; 2 4]. Then ad - bc = 4 - 4 = 0, so B has no inverse. Notice the second row of B is twice the first, which is the real reason it is stuck.

Solving systems with an inverse: If A is invertible, the system Ax = b has exactly one solution, x = A^-1 b. Proof: multiply both sides on the left by A^-1 to get A^-1 A x = A^-1 b, which is I x = A^-1 b. Let us redo the bazar puzzle: 2p + q = 130 and p + 3q = 190, so A = [2 1; 1 3] and ad - bc = 6 - 1 = 5. Then A^-1 = (1/5)[3 -1; -1 2], and x = (1/5)(3(130) - 190, -130 + 2(190)) = (1/5)(200, 250) = (40, 50). Potatoes 40 taka, onions 50 taka, same as before.

A practical warning: Using x = A^-1 b is great for theory and for small hand problems, and also handy when you must solve Ax = b for many different b with the same A. But for a single large system, computing A^-1 is slower and less accurate than plain elimination or LU decomposition. Numerical programmers have a saying: you almost never need to actually compute the inverse. In NumPy, for example, people use numpy.linalg.solve(A, b) rather than inv(A) @ b.

Finding inverses with Gauss-Jordan: For bigger matrices, there is a neat trick. Write A and I side by side as one wide matrix [A | I]. Row reduce the whole thing with Gauss-Jordan. If the left half turns into I, then the right half has become A^-1, so [A | I] becomes [I | A^-1]. If the left half ever gets a row of all zeros, A has no inverse and you can stop. Why does this work? Each row operation is secretly a multiplication on the left. The operations that turn A into I multiply together to give A^-1, and applying them to I just records that product.

A 3 by 3 example, part 1: Let A have rows [1 2 3], [0 1 4], [5 6 0]. Start with [A | I], whose rows are [1 2 3 | 1 0 0], [0 1 4 | 0 1 0], [5 6 0 | 0 0 1]. The first pivot is 1. Row 2 already has a 0 below it. Kill the 5: R3 -> R3 - 5 R1 gives [0 -4 -15 | -5 0 1]. Now the second pivot is the 1 in row 2. Kill the -4 below it: R3 -> R3 + 4 R2 gives [0 0 1 | -5 4 1]. The left side is now upper triangular with pivots 1, 1, 1.

A 3 by 3 example, part 2: Now clear upward. R2 -> R2 - 4 R3 gives [0 1 0 | 0 + 20, 1 - 16, 0 - 4] = [0 1 0 | 20 -15 -4]. R1 -> R1 - 3 R3 gives [1 2 0 | 1 + 15, -12, -3] = [1 2 0 | 16 -12 -3]. Finally R1 -> R1 - 2 R2 gives [1 0 0 | 16 - 40, -12 + 30, -3 + 8] = [1 0 0 | -24 18 5]. So A^-1 has rows [-24 18 5], [20 -15 -4], [-5 4 1].

Checking the 3 by 3 answer: Multiply A by this matrix. Row 1 of A, [1 2 3], times column 1, (-24, 20, -5), gives -24 + 40 - 15 = 1. Row 1 times column 2, (18, -15, 4), gives 18 - 30 + 12 = 0. Row 3 of A, [5 6 0], times column 1 gives -120 + 120 + 0 = 0, and times column 3, (5, -4, 1), gives 25 - 24 + 0 = 1. Doing all nine gives the identity. In an exam, checking even two or three entries is a quick way to catch a slip.

Properties of inverses: If A and B are invertible n by n matrices and k is a nonzero number, then: (A^-1)^-1 = A, undoing the undo gets you back. (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, with the order reversed, exactly like socks and shoes. (A^T)^-1 = (A^-1)^T, so transpose and inverse can be done in either order. (kA)^-1 = (1/k) A^-1. And (A^n)^-1 = (A^-1)^n. Check the socks-and-shoes rule: (AB)(B^-1 A^-1) = A(B B^-1)A^-1 = A I A^-1 = A A^-1 = I.

Cancellation needs care: With numbers, if ab = ac and a is not 0, then b = c. With matrices, if AB = AC and A is invertible, you can multiply on the left by A^-1 and get B = C. But if A is singular, this can fail: two different matrices B and C can give the same product. Also, the product of two nonzero matrices can be the zero matrix. These surprises are exactly why invertibility matters so much.

Elementary matrices: An elementary matrix is what you get by doing one elementary row operation to the identity matrix. For example, doing R2 -> R2 - 2 R1 to the 2 by 2 identity gives E = [1 0; -2 1]. The magic fact: multiplying any matrix A on the left by E performs that same row operation on A. Try A = [1 3; 2 5]: EA = [1 3; 2 - 2, 5 - 6] = [1 3; 0 -1]. That is exactly R2 -> R2 - 2 R1. Every row operation in elimination is really a left multiplication by an elementary matrix.

Elementary matrices are invertible: Every row operation can be undone by another row operation, so every elementary matrix has an inverse that is also elementary. The inverse of E = [1 0; -2 1] is [1 0; 2 1], which adds back 2 times row 1. A swap matrix is its own inverse. Scaling a row by k is undone by scaling by 1/k. Now if Gauss-Jordan turns A into I using E1, E2, ..., Ek, then Ek ... E2 E1 A = I, which means A^-1 = Ek ... E2 E1 and A = E1^-1 E2^-1 ... Ek^-1. So an invertible matrix is a product of elementary matrices.

The invertible matrix theorem, introduction: For a square n by n matrix A, the following statements are all equivalent, meaning if one is true they are all true, and if one is false they are all false. A is invertible. The RREF of A is I. A has n pivots. Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b. A is a product of elementary matrices. A^T is invertible. The columns of A are linearly independent. The determinant of A is not 0. Later lessons will add more items, such as the columns spanning R^n and 0 not being an eigenvalue.

Real life example 1, secret messages: The Hill cipher, invented by Lester Hill in 1929, encodes a message using a matrix. Turn letters into numbers (A = 0, B = 1, and so on), group them into small vectors, and multiply each vector by a key matrix K, working modulo 26. Your friend decodes by multiplying by the inverse of K, also modulo 26. If K has no inverse mod 26, the message cannot be decoded at all, so choosing an invertible key is essential. The Hill cipher is far too weak for real security today, but it shows clearly how an inverse means the ability to undo.

Real life example 2, undo in graphics: When you rotate and scale a photo in an editing app or a filter on your phone, the app applies a transformation matrix to the coordinates of every pixel. To map points on the finished image back to the original photo, or to let you undo, the software uses the inverse matrix. In 3D games, the camera's view is built with the inverse of the camera's own position-and-rotation matrix. And when a transformation squashes everything onto a line, like a matrix with determinant 0, information is lost and there is no way to undo it.

Common mistakes: Writing (AB)^-1 = A^-1 B^-1, when the correct order is B^-1 A^-1. Forgetting the 1/(ad - bc) factor in the 2 by 2 formula, or swapping a and d but forgetting to change the signs of b and c. Taking the inverse of each entry, which is completely wrong. Trying to invert a non-square matrix. Writing B/A instead of A^-1 B or B A^-1, which hides which side you multiply on, and the side matters. In Gauss-Jordan, doing row operations on the left half only and forgetting the right half.

What exams ask: Find the inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix with the formula and verify it. Find the inverse of a 3 by 3 matrix by Gauss-Jordan elimination, or show that it does not exist. Solve a system using x = A^-1 b. Prove that the inverse is unique, or that (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1. Write the elementary matrix for a given row operation, or write A as a product of elementary matrices. Use the invertible matrix theorem to decide several statements at once. For which k is [1 k; 2 6] invertible? Here ad - bc = 6 - 2k, so it is invertible for every k except k = 3.

Recap: A square matrix A is invertible when some A^-1 satisfies A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I, and that inverse is unique. For 2 by 2, swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal and divide by ad - bc, which must not be 0. For larger matrices, row reduce [A | I] to [I | A^-1]. Inverses reverse the order of products, and every row operation is a multiplication by an invertible elementary matrix. The invertible matrix theorem ties invertibility to pivots, unique solutions and much more. Next lesson, LU decomposition, shows how computers actually solve systems efficiently without computing inverses.
key_points: A square A is invertible if A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I; otherwise it is singular.
The inverse is unique; never divide by a matrix, multiply by its inverse on the correct side.
2 x 2: [a b; c d]^-1 = (1/(ad - bc)) [d -b; -c a], only when ad - bc != 0.
If A is invertible, Ax = b has exactly one solution x = A^-1 b.
Gauss-Jordan method: row reduce [A | I] to [I | A^-1]; a zero row on the left means no inverse.
An elementary matrix does one row operation; EA applies that operation to A, and E is always invertible.
Invertible matrix theorem: invertible <=> RREF is I <=> n pivots <=> Ax = 0 only trivial <=> det != 0.
lessons.tip: Always multiply your answer by the original matrix to check you get I. For a 3 x 3 inverse, even checking the diagonal entries and one off-diagonal entry catches most mistakes in under a minute.
lessons.task: On paper, find the inverse of [3 5; 1 2] with the 2 x 2 formula, then find it again with Gauss-Jordan on [A | I]. Both answers must match. Use it to solve 3x + 5y = 11, x + 2y = 4, and check your x and y in the original equations.

quiz.q: What is the inverse of [3 1; 5 2]?
quiz.explain: ad - bc = 6 - 5 = 1, so swap the diagonal and negate the off-diagonal: [2 -1; -5 3].

quiz.q: For invertible A and B, what is (AB)^-1?
quiz.explain: Inverses reverse the order, like taking off shoes before socks.

quiz.q: Which matrix has no inverse?
quiz.explain: For [2 6; 1 3], ad - bc = 6 - 6 = 0, so it is singular.

quiz.q: While row reducing [A | I] for a 3 x 3 A, the left side gets a row of zeros. What does it mean?
options: You must swap the two halves
quiz.explain: A zero row on the left means fewer than 3 pivots, so A is singular.

quiz.q: A is 4 x 4 and Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. What follows?
options: Ax = b has no solution for some b
quiz.explain: By the invertible matrix theorem, only the trivial solution means A is invertible.

lessons.title: LU Decomposition and Computation
lessons.content:
Imagine a rice mill in Naogaon that uses the same three machines every day. The way the machines share the work never changes, but the daily orders do. On Sunday the shops want one mix of rice, on Monday another, on Tuesday another. If the manager had to redo the whole planning from scratch every morning, she would waste hours. A clever manager does the hard thinking once, writes it down, and then each new order takes only a minute. LU decomposition is exactly that trick for systems of linear equations: do the expensive elimination work on the matrix A once, save it, and then solve Ax = b quickly for as many different b's as you like.

Where we are in the course: In the Gaussian elimination lesson you learned to turn a system into an upper triangular one and then use back substitution. In the inverse lesson you saw how to find A^-1. This lesson shows how real computers actually solve Ax = b. They almost never compute the inverse. Instead they factor A into two triangular pieces, L and U, and solve two easy triangular systems.

What LU means: LU decomposition (also called LU factorization) writes a square matrix A as a product A = LU, where L is lower triangular (all zeros above the main diagonal) and U is upper triangular (all zeros below the main diagonal). In the most common version, called Doolittle form, L has 1s on its diagonal. U is simply the echelon form you get from Gaussian elimination, and L is a neat record of the multipliers you used along the way.

Why triangular is great: A triangular system is the easiest kind of system to solve. If the matrix is upper triangular, the last equation has only one unknown, so you solve it, plug it into the equation above, and climb upwards. That is back substitution. If the matrix is lower triangular, the first equation has only one unknown, so you solve it and go downwards. That is forward substitution. No row operations are needed at all, just one division per unknown and some multiply-and-subtract steps.

A worked example, the elimination part: Take A with rows [2 1 1], [4 3 3], [8 7 9]. The first pivot is 2. To kill the 4 below it, subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2, giving [0 1 1]. The multiplier is 2. To kill the 8, subtract 4 times row 1 from row 3, giving [0 3 5]. The multiplier is 4. Now the second pivot is 1. To kill the 3 below it, subtract 3 times the new row 2 from row 3, giving [0 0 2]. The multiplier is 3. We have reached U with rows [2 1 1], [0 1 1], [0 0 2].

Building L for free: Here is the beautiful part. L is just the identity matrix with each multiplier placed in the spot it was used to clear. The multiplier 2 cleared position (2,1), the 4 cleared (3,1) and the 3 cleared (3,2). So L has rows [1 0 0], [2 1 0], [4 3 1]. You do not need any extra work to find L. You only need to remember the numbers you already used. Notice the sign: we subtracted multiples, and the multipliers go into L with a plus sign.

Checking that A = LU: Multiply L by U row by row. Row 1 of LU is 1 times [2 1 1], which is [2 1 1]. Row 2 is 2 times [2 1 1] plus 1 times [0 1 1], which is [4 3 3]. Row 3 is 4 times [2 1 1] plus 3 times [0 1 1] plus 1 times [0 0 2], which is [8 4 4] + [0 3 3] + [0 0 2] = [8 7 9]. That is exactly A. The multipliers in L tell you how to rebuild each row of A from the rows of U.

Solving Ax = b with L and U: Since A = LU, the equation Ax = b becomes L(Ux) = b. Give the inside a name, y = Ux. Then solve in two steps. Step 1, forward substitution: solve Ly = b for y. Step 2, back substitution: solve Ux = y for x. Two easy triangular solves replace one hard general solve.

Example with b = (4, 10, 24): Forward substitution with L: the first row says y1 = 4. The second row says 2 y1 + y2 = 10, so y2 = 10 - 8 = 2. The third row says 4 y1 + 3 y2 + y3 = 24, so y3 = 24 - 16 - 6 = 2. So y = (4, 2, 2). Back substitution with U: the last row says 2 x3 = 2, so x3 = 1. The middle row says x2 + x3 = 2, so x2 = 1. The top row says 2 x1 + x2 + x3 = 4, so 2 x1 = 2 and x1 = 1. The answer is x = (1, 1, 1). Check: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, 4 + 3 + 3 = 10, 8 + 7 + 9 = 24. Correct.

A second order on the same day: Now the right side changes to b = (3, 7, 17). We do not touch A again. Forward: y1 = 3, y2 = 7 - 2(3) = 1, y3 = 17 - 4(3) - 3(1) = 2. Back: 2 x3 = 2 gives x3 = 1, x2 + 1 = 1 gives x2 = 0, 2 x1 + 0 + 1 = 3 gives x1 = 1. So x = (1, 0, 1). Check: 2 + 0 + 1 = 3, 4 + 0 + 3 = 7, 8 + 0 + 9 = 17. That is the whole point: the second solve cost only a handful of multiplications.

Counting the cost: Computer scientists measure numerical work in flops, meaning basic floating point operations like one multiply or one add. For an n x n matrix, the elimination that produces L and U costs about (2/3) n^3 flops. Each forward substitution costs about n^2 flops and each back substitution about n^2 flops, so one full solve with an existing LU costs about 2 n^2. For n = 1000, factoring costs roughly 670 million flops, while each extra solve costs only about 2 million. That is over 300 times cheaper. If you have 100 different b vectors, you factor once and pay the small price 100 times.

Why not just compute A^-1: You could find A^-1 once and then compute x = A^-1 b for each b, which also costs about 2 n^2 per b. But computing the inverse costs about 2 n^3 flops, roughly three times the cost of LU, and the answers are usually a little less accurate because more rounding happens. That is why numerical analysts repeat the rule: do not invert a matrix to solve a system. In code, numpy.linalg.solve and MATLAB's backslash operator do not form the inverse; for a general square matrix they use LU factorization with partial pivoting from the LAPACK library.

When plain LU fails: Elimination divides by pivots. If a pivot is zero, you are stuck. The matrix with rows [0 1] and [1 1] is perfectly invertible, yet it has no LU factorization in Doolittle form because the very first pivot is 0. The fix is to swap rows first. A row swap can be recorded with a permutation matrix P, which is the identity with its rows rearranged. Then the honest statement is PA = LU. Every invertible square matrix has a factorization of this form.

Partial pivoting, the real reason: Even a pivot that is not exactly zero can cause trouble if it is tiny. Computers round every number to a fixed number of digits. Suppose we keep only 3 significant digits and solve 0.0001 x1 + x2 = 1, x1 + x2 = 2. The true answer is about x1 = 1.0001, x2 = 0.9999. Without swapping, the multiplier is 10000. Row 2 becomes (1 - 10000) x2 = 2 - 10000, which rounds to -10000 x2 = -10000, so x2 = 1. Then 0.0001 x1 + 1 = 1 gives x1 = 0. That is badly wrong. With partial pivoting we first swap so the bigger number 1 is the pivot. The multiplier becomes 0.0001, row 2 becomes about 1.00 x2 = 1.00, so x2 = 1, and then x1 = 2 - 1 = 1. Correct to 3 digits.

The partial pivoting rule: Before eliminating in a column, look down that column from the pivot position, find the entry with the largest absolute value, and swap its row up to the pivot position. This keeps every multiplier between -1 and 1, which stops rounding errors from blowing up in almost all practical problems. The extra cost is just comparing numbers, which is tiny next to the n^3 arithmetic.

Saving memory: A computer does not need two separate arrays for L and U. The diagonal of L is all 1s, so it does not need storing, and the multipliers can be written into the zero spots below the diagonal of U as elimination goes. So a single n x n array holds the whole factorization, plus a small list that records the row swaps. For our example the packed array would have rows [2 1 1], [2 1 1], [4 3 2], where the lower part (2, 4, 3) is L and the upper part including the diagonal is U.

A free bonus, the determinant: Once you have PA = LU, the determinant of A is the product of the diagonal entries of U, with the sign flipped once for each row swap. For our example, det A = 2 x 1 x 2 = 4. You will learn why in the determinant lessons, but this is how software actually computes determinants: never by cofactor expansion, always through LU.

A cousin for special matrices: If A is symmetric and positive definite (this happens a lot in physics, statistics and machine learning), there is a faster factorization called Cholesky, A = L L^T, which costs about half as much as LU, roughly (1/3) n^3 flops. Just know the name for now; it is the same idea of splitting into triangular pieces.

Real-life example 1, simulating a circuit: Circuit simulators like SPICE turn a circuit into a big linear system using Kirchhoff's laws, where the unknowns are voltages at the nodes. When an engineer designing a phone charger wants to see what happens for many different input voltages, the circuit (the matrix A) stays the same while the sources (the vector b) change. The simulator factors A once and reuses L and U for every new input. The same idea appears in sparse LU solvers that handle matrices with millions of rows, where most entries are zero.

Real-life example 2, analysing a bridge: When engineers check a large structure such as a long river bridge, finite element software splits the structure into thousands of small pieces and builds a stiffness matrix K. The equation K u = f connects the forces f (traffic, wind, the weight of the bridge itself) to the movements u of every piece. Engineers test many load cases: a line of trucks on one side, strong monsoon wind, both together. K does not change between load cases, so the program factors it once and then runs a quick forward and back substitution for each case.

Common mistakes: Students often put the multipliers into L with the wrong sign, or in the wrong position. Remember, the multiplier that cleared row i, column j goes into L at position (i, j). Another mistake is forgetting that a row swap changes the problem: if you swap rows of A, you must swap the same entries of b, which is what P does in PAx = Pb. Some students also think every matrix has an LU factorization; without row swaps that is false, as the [0 1; 1 1] example shows.

What exams ask: Expect questions like: find the LU factorization of a given 3 x 3 matrix; use a given L and U to solve Ax = b by forward and back substitution; explain why LU is better than computing the inverse when there are many right-hand sides; state the flop counts (2/3) n^3 for factoring and about 2 n^2 per solve; show with a small example why partial pivoting is needed; or compute a determinant from U.

Recap: LU decomposition is Gaussian elimination with a memory. U is the echelon form, L stores the multipliers with 1s on its diagonal, and A = LU (or PA = LU with row swaps). To solve Ax = b, do forward substitution Ly = b, then back substitution Ux = y. Factoring costs about (2/3) n^3 flops once; each new right side costs only about 2 n^2. Partial pivoting keeps the arithmetic stable, and this is the method running inside almost every serious numerical library.
key_points: LU decomposition writes A = LU with L lower triangular (1s on the diagonal) and U upper triangular.
U is the echelon form from Gaussian elimination; L stores the multipliers in the positions they cleared.
To solve Ax = b: forward substitution for Ly = b, then back substitution for Ux = y.
Factoring costs about (2/3) n^3 flops once; each new right-hand side costs only about 2 n^2 flops.
Do not invert a matrix to solve a system: LU is cheaper and more accurate.
Zero or tiny pivots need row swaps; with partial pivoting the factorization is PA = LU.
The determinant equals the product of U's diagonal, with a sign change for each row swap.
lessons.tip: Always multiply L and U back together at the end of a hand calculation. It takes one minute and catches almost every sign or position mistake in the multipliers.
lessons.task: Take A with rows [1 2], [3 8]. On paper find L and U (one multiplier). Then use them to solve Ax = b for b = (5, 19) and for b = (3, 11), and check each answer by plugging it back into A.

quiz.q: In the Doolittle LU factorization A = LU, what is on the diagonal of L?
quiz.explain: In Doolittle form L is unit lower triangular, so every diagonal entry of L is 1 and the pivots sit on U's diagonal.

quiz.q: To solve Ax = b using A = LU, which order is correct?
options: Solve Ly = b by forward substitution, then Ux = y by back substitution
Solve Ux = b first, then Ly = x
Compute L^-1 and U^-1 and multiply them
quiz.explain: L(Ux) = b, so first find y = Ux from Ly = b going downwards, then find x from Ux = y going upwards.

quiz.q: For a large n x n matrix, about how many flops does the LU factorization cost?
quiz.explain: Elimination costs about (2/3) n^3 flops; each later triangular solve pair costs only about 2 n^2.

quiz.q: Why is partial pivoting used?
options: To avoid zero or tiny pivots that cause large rounding errors
quiz.explain: Swapping the largest entry into the pivot keeps multipliers at most 1 in size, which stops rounding errors from growing.

quiz.q: A = LU with U having diagonal 3, 2, 5 and no row swaps. What is det A?
quiz.explain: det A = det L x det U = 1 x (3 x 2 x 5) = 30.

lessons.title: Determinants I: Computing Determinants
lessons.content:
Imagine every square matrix carries a little secret number in its pocket. You cannot see it by looking at one entry, but it is built from all of them together. That number tells you, in one shot, whether the matrix can be undone, whether a system Ax = b has exactly one solution, and how much the matrix stretches areas and volumes. This secret number is called the determinant, written det(A) or |A|. In this lesson we learn how to calculate it. In the next lesson we learn its rules and what it means.

What a determinant is: The determinant is a function that takes a square matrix (n x n, never a rectangle) and gives back a single number. A 2 x 3 matrix has no determinant at all. The headline fact, which we will explain properly in the next lesson, is simple: A is invertible exactly when det(A) is not zero. If det(A) = 0, the matrix is singular, it squashes space flat, and Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many.

The 1 x 1 case: For a 1 x 1 matrix [a], the determinant is just a. The equation a x = b has a unique solution exactly when a is not 0. That is the whole idea in its smallest form.

The 2 x 2 formula: For A with rows [a b] and [c d], det(A) = ad - bc. Multiply down the main diagonal, multiply down the other diagonal, and subtract. Example: rows [3 1] and [2 4] give 3 x 4 - 1 x 2 = 12 - 2 = 10. Another: rows [2 6] and [1 3] give 6 - 6 = 0, and indeed row 1 is just twice row 2, so the matrix is singular.

Where ad - bc comes from: Solve ax + by = e, cx + dy = f by elimination. Multiply the first equation by d and the second by b and subtract: (ad - bc) x = ed - bf. So x can be found by dividing by ad - bc, which only works if ad - bc is not zero. The determinant appears naturally the moment you try to solve a 2 x 2 system. Remember the bazar system from the systems lesson, 2p + q = 130, p + 3q = 190: its determinant is 2 x 3 - 1 x 1 = 5, not zero, which is why it had exactly one answer.

The 3 x 3 case with Sarrus: For a 3 x 3 matrix there is a handy picture called the rule of Sarrus. Copy the first two columns to the right of the matrix. Then add the three products going down to the right, and subtract the three products going up to the right (or equivalently, going down to the left). Take A with rows [1 2 3], [0 4 5], [1 0 6]. Down-right products: 1 x 4 x 6 = 24, 2 x 5 x 1 = 10, 3 x 0 x 0 = 0, total 34. The other three: 3 x 4 x 1 = 12, 1 x 5 x 0 = 0, 2 x 0 x 6 = 0, total 12. So det(A) = 34 - 12 = 22.

A warning about Sarrus: The rule of Sarrus works only for 3 x 3 matrices. There is no diagonal trick like it for 4 x 4 or larger. Students who try to stretch it to 4 x 4 get wrong answers every year. For bigger matrices we need a method that works for every size: cofactor expansion.

Minors: Pick an entry a_ij in row i and column j. Cross out row i and column j. What is left is a smaller (n - 1) x (n - 1) matrix, and its determinant is called the minor M_ij. In our 3 x 3 example, crossing out row 1 and column 1 leaves rows [4 5] and [0 6], so M_11 = 24 - 0 = 24. Crossing out row 1 and column 2 leaves [0 5] and [1 6], so M_12 = 0 - 5 = -5.

Cofactors: A cofactor is a minor with a sign attached: C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij. The sign follows a checkerboard pattern starting with plus in the top-left corner. For a 3 x 3 matrix the signs are: + - + in row 1, - + - in row 2, + - + in row 3. So C_11 = +24 and C_12 = -(-5) = +5. The sign depends only on the position, never on the entry itself.

Cofactor expansion (Laplace expansion): Choose any row or any column. Multiply each entry by its cofactor, and add them up. The result is the determinant, and it is the same whichever row or column you choose. Along row 1 of our example: det(A) = 1 x C_11 + 2 x C_12 + 3 x C_13. We have C_11 = 24 and C_12 = 5. For C_13, cross out row 1 and column 3, leaving [0 4] and [1 0], minor 0 - 4 = -4, sign plus, so C_13 = -4. Then det(A) = 24 + 10 - 12 = 22. Same answer as Sarrus.

Choose the row with the most zeros: Because every row and column gives the same result, a smart student picks the one with the most zeros, since a zero entry kills its whole term. In our example, column 1 has entries 1, 0, 1. Expanding along it: 1 x (+M_11) + 0 x (whatever) + 1 x (+M_31). M_31 comes from crossing out row 3 and column 1, leaving [2 3] and [4 5], which is 10 - 12 = -2. Position (3,1) has sign plus. So det(A) = 24 + 0 - 2 = 22. Fewer terms, same answer.

A 4 x 4 example: Take A with rows [1 0 2 0], [3 1 0 0], [0 0 2 0], [4 0 1 5]. Column 4 has only one non-zero entry, the 5 at position (4,4), with sign plus. So det(A) = 5 x M_44, where M_44 is the determinant of rows [1 0 2], [3 1 0], [0 0 2]. Expand that along its row 3, which has only the 2 at position (3,3), sign plus: 2 x det of [1 0] and [3 1], which is 2 x 1 = 2. So det(A) = 5 x 2 = 10. With good choices, a scary 4 x 4 becomes two tiny steps.

How cofactor expansion grows: Expanding an n x n matrix gives n determinants of size n - 1, each of those gives n - 1 of size n - 2, and so on. In the worst case you end up adding about n! products. For n = 10 that is 3,628,800 products. For n = 20 it is about 2.4 x 10^18, which would take a fast computer years. That is why cofactor expansion is great for hand calculations with small or sparse matrices, but useless for big ones. Real software uses row reduction, as you saw at the end of the LU lesson.

The big formula, just so you know: If you keep expanding all the way, you get the permutation formula. The determinant is a sum of n! terms. Each term picks exactly one entry from every row and every column, multiplies them, and attaches a plus or minus sign depending on how the column choices are shuffled. For 2 x 2 the two terms are ad and -bc. For 3 x 3 there are six terms, which are exactly the six diagonals of Sarrus. You do not need to compute with this formula, but it explains why both methods agree.

Triangular matrices are easy: If A is upper or lower triangular, its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries. Example: rows [2 5 7], [0 3 1], [0 0 4] give det = 2 x 3 x 4 = 24. Why? Expand along the first column: only the 2 survives, leaving a smaller triangular matrix, and you repeat. The off-diagonal numbers 5, 7 and 1 never matter. Diagonal matrices are a special case, and so is the identity: det(I) = 1.

Quick zero tests: A few patterns give det = 0 immediately. If a row or column is all zeros, expand along it and every term is zero. If two rows are equal, or one row is a multiple of another, the determinant is zero, because the rows do not point in truly different directions (you will prove this with row operations next lesson). Spotting these saves a lot of work in exams.

Real-life example 1, which way does a triangle turn: Game engines and map apps constantly need to know whether three points A, B, C go around counterclockwise or clockwise. Make two vectors, B - A and C - A, put them as rows of a 2 x 2 matrix, and take the determinant. Positive means counterclockwise, negative means clockwise, zero means the three points are on one straight line. For A = (0, 0), B = (4, 0), C = (0, 3), the matrix has rows [4 0] and [0 3], determinant 12, so the turn is counterclockwise. A ride-sharing app checking if a road bends left or right, or a game deciding which side of a triangle faces the camera, uses exactly this 2 x 2 determinant.

Real-life example 2, checking before solving: Suppose a small shop in Chattogram tracks two products with two equations from two days of sales, and an inventory program wants to solve for the prices automatically. Before dividing by anything, the program can compute the 2 x 2 determinant. If it is zero, the two days gave the same kind of information (for example, day 2 is just day 1 doubled), so the prices cannot be pinned down, and the program warns the user to collect a different day's data instead of crashing or printing nonsense.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the checkerboard signs is the number one error, especially the minus at positions like (1,2) and (2,1). Second is using Sarrus on a 4 x 4. Third is computing a minor by crossing out the wrong row or column. Fourth is thinking a determinant exists for non-square matrices. Fifth is mixing up the vertical bars |A| for determinant with absolute value; a determinant can be negative, like det of rows [0 1] and [1 0], which is -1.

What exams ask: Typical questions: compute a 2 x 2 or 3 x 3 determinant; find a specific minor and cofactor; expand a 4 x 4 along the best row or column; find the value of k that makes a matrix singular (set det = 0 and solve, for example rows [k 2] and [3 6] give 6k - 6 = 0, so k = 1); show that a triangular matrix's determinant is the product of its diagonal; and explain why cofactor expansion is too slow for large n.

Recap: The determinant is one number attached to a square matrix. For 2 x 2 it is ad - bc. For 3 x 3 you can use Sarrus, but only there. In general, use cofactor expansion: minor M_ij by deleting row i and column j, cofactor C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij, then sum entry times cofactor along any row or column, choosing the one with most zeros. Triangular matrices just multiply their diagonal. Cofactor expansion costs about n! work, so computers use elimination instead. Next lesson: how row operations change the determinant, det(AB), the adjoint, Cramer's rule and the meaning of area and volume.
key_points: The determinant is a single number defined only for square matrices; A is invertible exactly when det(A) is not 0.
For 2 x 2, det = ad - bc.
Sarrus' diagonal rule works for 3 x 3 only, never for 4 x 4 or bigger.
Minor M_ij: delete row i and column j; cofactor C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij with checkerboard signs.
Cofactor expansion along any row or column gives the same value, so pick the one with the most zeros.
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries; det(I) = 1.
Cofactor expansion takes about n! work, so it is for hand calculation only.
lessons.tip: Before you start expanding, spend five seconds looking for the row or column with the most zeros, and write the checkerboard of + and - signs in the margin. Those two habits remove most mistakes.
lessons.task: Pick any 3 x 3 matrix of small whole numbers (or take rows [2 1 0], [1 3 1], [0 1 4]). Compute its determinant three ways: Sarrus, expansion along row 1, and expansion along column 3. All three should match. (For the given matrix the answer is 18.)

quiz.q: What is the determinant of the matrix with rows [5 2] and [3 4]?
For which matrix sizes does the rule of Sarrus work?
quiz.explain: Sarrus' diagonal trick matches the six terms of a 3 x 3 determinant; it gives wrong answers for 4 x 4 and up.

quiz.q: What is the sign of the cofactor at position (2,3)?
options: Always the sign of the entry
quiz.explain: C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij, and 2 + 3 = 5 is odd, so the sign is minus.

quiz.q: What is the determinant of the triangular matrix with rows [3 8 1], [0 2 9], [0 0 5]?
quiz.explain: For a triangular matrix multiply the diagonal: 3 x 2 x 5 = 30.

quiz.q: For which k is the matrix with rows [k 4] and [2 8] singular?
quiz.explain: det = 8k - 8, which is 0 when k = 1.

lessons.title: Determinants II: Properties, Cramer's Rule and Meaning
lessons.content:
Last lesson you learned how to calculate a determinant: ad - bc, Sarrus, and cofactor expansion. That is like learning how to weigh a bag of rice. This lesson is about what the weight tells you and the shortcuts that make weighing easy. We will see how row operations change the determinant, why det(AB) = det(A) det(B), how the determinant builds the inverse through the adjoint, how Cramer's rule solves systems with determinants alone, and the beautiful geometric meaning: the determinant is the factor by which a matrix scales area and volume.

Rule 1, swapping two rows flips the sign: If B is A with two rows swapped, then det(B) = -det(A). Check with rows [1 2] and [3 4]: det = 4 - 6 = -2. Swap them to [3 4] and [1 2]: det = 6 - 4 = 2. The sign flipped, the size stayed. A neat consequence: if two rows of A are equal, swapping them gives the same matrix but must flip the sign, so det(A) = -det(A), which forces det(A) = 0.

Rule 2, multiplying a row by k multiplies the determinant by k: If you multiply one row by 3, the determinant becomes 3 times as big. Rows [1 2] and [3 4] have det -2. Change the first row to [3 6] and the determinant is 12 - 18 = -6, which is 3 x (-2). This also means you can pull a common factor out of a row: the determinant of rows [4 8] and [1 5] equals 4 times the determinant of rows [1 2] and [1 5], which is 4 x 3 = 12. Check directly: 20 - 8 = 12.

Rule 3, adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing: This is the most useful rule. Replacing row i with row i plus k times row j leaves the determinant exactly the same. Rows [1 2] and [3 4]: subtract 3 times row 1 from row 2 to get [1 2] and [0 -2]. The determinant is 1 x (-2) - 0 = -2, unchanged. Since Gaussian elimination mostly uses this operation, elimination keeps the determinant safe.

Computing determinants by row reduction: Combine the three rules with the triangular rule (product of the diagonal). Reduce A to upper triangular form, keep track of any swaps and scalings, then multiply the diagonal. Take A with rows [2 4 2], [1 3 4], [3 7 9]. Subtract 0.5 times row 1 from row 2: [0 1 3]. Subtract 1.5 times row 1 from row 3: [0 1 6]. Subtract row 2 from row 3: [0 0 3]. Only rule 3 was used, so det(A) = 2 x 1 x 3 = 6. Cofactor expansion agrees: 2(27 - 28) - 4(9 - 12) + 2(7 - 9) = -2 + 12 - 4 = 6. For an n x n matrix this costs about n^3 operations instead of n!, which is exactly how LU gives the determinant.

Columns behave the same way: The determinant of the transpose equals the determinant: det(A^T) = det(A). Since transposing turns rows into columns, every rule about rows also holds for columns. A zero column gives det 0, two equal columns give det 0, and swapping two columns flips the sign.

Rule for products, det(AB) = det(A) det(B): This is one of the most surprising facts in the course. Take A with rows [1 2] and [3 4], det -2, and B with rows [2 0] and [1 3], det 6. Then AB has rows [4 6] and [10 12], whose determinant is 48 - 60 = -12, exactly -2 x 6. Some consequences follow at once. det(A^2) = det(A)^2. det(A^-1) = 1 / det(A), because A A^-1 = I and det(I) = 1. And det(AB) = det(BA), even though AB and BA are usually different matrices.

What does NOT work: The determinant does not split over addition. In general det(A + B) is not det(A) + det(B). With the A and B above, A + B has rows [3 2] and [4 7], det = 21 - 8 = 13, but det(A) + det(B) = -2 + 6 = 4. Also, det(kA) is not k det(A). Multiplying the whole n x n matrix by k multiplies every one of the n rows by k, so det(kA) = k^n det(A). For a 3 x 3 matrix, det(2A) = 8 det(A).

The invertibility test: Putting everything together: A is invertible if and only if det(A) is not zero. Reason: row reduction changes the determinant only by non-zero factors (sign flips and non-zero scalings), so det(A) is zero exactly when the reduced triangular form has a zero on its diagonal, which means a missing pivot, which means A is not invertible. This test joins the list of equivalent conditions in the invertible matrix theorem: det(A) not 0, A has n pivots, Ax = 0 has only the zero solution, and Ax = b has a unique solution for every b.

The adjoint (adjugate): Make a matrix of all the cofactors C_ij, then transpose it. The result is called the adjoint or adjugate of A, written adj(A). The key identity is A adj(A) = det(A) I. Why? Multiplying row i of A by column i of adj(A) is a cofactor expansion along row i, which gives det(A). Multiplying row i of A by a different column gives the expansion of a matrix with two equal rows, which is 0. So if det(A) is not zero, A^-1 = adj(A) / det(A).

The 2 x 2 adjoint: For rows [a b] and [c d], the cofactors are C_11 = d, C_12 = -c, C_21 = -b, C_22 = a. Transposing gives adj(A) with rows [d -b] and [-c a]. So A^-1 = (1 / (ad - bc)) times rows [d -b] and [-c a]. That is the 2 x 2 inverse formula you met in the inverse lesson; now you know where it comes from: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant.

A 3 x 3 adjoint example: Take A with rows [1 2 3], [0 1 4], [5 6 0]. Expanding along row 1: det(A) = 1(0 - 24) - 2(0 - 20) + 3(0 - 5) = -24 + 40 - 15 = 1. The nine cofactors are C_11 = -24, C_12 = 20, C_13 = -5, C_21 = 18, C_22 = -15, C_23 = 4, C_31 = 5, C_32 = -4, C_33 = 1. Transposing, adj(A) has rows [-24 18 5], [20 -15 -4], [-5 4 1]. Since det(A) = 1, this is A^-1. Check one entry: row 1 of A times column 1 of adj(A) is -24 + 40 - 15 = 1, as it should be. The adjoint method is fine for 3 x 3 by hand, but for big matrices Gauss-Jordan or LU is far faster.

Cramer's rule: For a square system Ax = b with det(A) not zero, each unknown has a ready-made formula: x_i = det(A_i) / det(A), where A_i is A with its column i replaced by b. Back to the bazar: 2p + q = 130, p + 3q = 190. det(A) = 6 - 1 = 5. Replace column 1 by b: rows [130 1] and [190 3], determinant 390 - 190 = 200, so p = 200 / 5 = 40. Replace column 2 by b: rows [2 130] and [1 190], determinant 380 - 130 = 250, so q = 250 / 5 = 50. The same 40 and 50 taka as before.

When to use Cramer's rule: Cramer's rule is lovely for 2 x 2 and 3 x 3 systems, for proofs, and when you only need one unknown out of many. But solving an n x n system this way needs n + 1 determinants, which is far more work than one elimination for large n. It also does nothing for systems where det(A) = 0; then you must go back to row reduction to tell whether there are no solutions or infinitely many.

Geometric meaning, area: Put two vectors u = (3, 1) and v = (1, 2) in the plane. They make a parallelogram. Its area is the absolute value of the determinant of the matrix with u and v as columns (or rows): |3 x 2 - 1 x 1| = 5. A triangle using the same two edges has half that area, 2.5. For a triangle with corners (1, 1), (4, 2) and (2, 5), take edge vectors (3, 1) and (1, 4): determinant 12 - 1 = 11, so the area is 5.5.

Geometric meaning, volume and scaling: In 3D, three vectors make a slanted box called a parallelepiped, and its volume is the absolute value of the 3 x 3 determinant of those vectors. More generally, a matrix A acting on space multiplies every area (in 2D) or volume (in 3D) by |det(A)|. The matrix with rows [2 0] and [0 3] stretches x by 2 and y by 3, so a unit square becomes a 2 by 3 rectangle with area 6, and the determinant is 6. A determinant of 0 means the matrix flattens the plane onto a line or a point, which is why such a matrix cannot be undone.

What the sign means: The sign of the determinant tells whether the matrix keeps orientation or flips it like a mirror. A rotation has determinant +1: it keeps size and handedness. A reflection across the x-axis, rows [1 0] and [0 -1], has determinant -1: same size, but a left hand becomes a right hand. This also explains det(AB) = det(A) det(B): doing B then A scales area by det(B) and then by det(A).

Real-life example 1, measuring a land plot: Land surveyors (amins) in Bangladesh often have the corner coordinates of a plot. The shoelace formula, which is really a sum of 2 x 2 determinants, gives the area. For a four-cornered plot with corners (0, 0), (30, 0), (40, 20) and (0, 25) in metres, add x_i y_(i+1) - x_(i+1) y_i around the corners: 0 + (600 - 0) + (1000 - 0) + 0 = 1600. Half of it is 800 square metres. Since one decimal (shotangsho) is about 40.47 square metres, the plot is about 19.8 decimals. The same formula runs inside GIS and mapping software.

Real-life example 2, graphics and physics engines: A game engine stores each object's transform as a matrix. It checks the determinant all the time. If det is negative, the object has been mirrored, so the engine must flip which side of each triangle counts as the front, otherwise the model looks inside out. If det is close to zero, the object has been squashed nearly flat, and inverting the transform (needed for lighting and collision) would be unstable, so the engine warns or skips it. In physics and probability, the same scaling idea appears as the Jacobian determinant when changing variables in an integral.

Common mistakes: Writing det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B), which is false. Writing det(kA) = k det(A) instead of k^n det(A). Forgetting to flip the sign after a row swap during reduction. Scaling a row to make a pivot 1 and forgetting to undo that factor. Using Cramer's rule when det(A) = 0. And reporting a negative area: area and volume are the absolute value of the determinant.

What exams ask: Find a determinant by row reduction, stating each rule used; given det(A) = 4 for a 3 x 3 matrix, find det(2A), det(A^-1), det(A^T) and det(A^3) (answers 32, 1/4, 4 and 64); find adj(A) and A^-1 for a 3 x 3 matrix; solve a 2 x 2 or 3 x 3 system with Cramer's rule; find the area of a triangle or parallelogram from coordinates; or prove that a matrix with two equal rows has determinant zero.

Recap: Row swap flips the sign, scaling a row scales the determinant, adding a multiple of a row changes nothing. det(A^T) = det(A), det(AB) = det(A) det(B), det(A^-1) = 1 / det(A), det(kA) = k^n det(A), but det(A + B) has no simple rule. A is invertible exactly when det(A) is not 0, and then A^-1 = adj(A) / det(A). Cramer's rule gives x_i = det(A_i) / det(A). Geometrically, |det(A)| is how much A scales area or volume, and the sign says whether it flips orientation.
key_points: Row swap flips the sign; multiplying a row by k multiplies det by k; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged.
det(A^T) = det(A), det(AB) = det(A) det(B), det(A^-1) = 1/det(A), and det(kA) = k^n det(A) for n x n.
det(A + B) is generally not det(A) + det(B).
A is invertible exactly when det(A) is not 0.
adj(A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, and A^-1 = adj(A) / det(A).
Cramer's rule: x_i = det(A_i) / det(A), with column i of A replaced by b.
|det(A)| is the area or volume scale factor; a negative sign means orientation is flipped.
lessons.tip: When reducing a matrix to find its determinant, keep a small running note in the margin like 'x(-1) swap, x2 scaled'. At the end, undo those factors before multiplying the diagonal. Most lost marks come from forgetting one of them.
lessons.task: On graph paper (or in any notes app) pick three points that make a triangle, for example (1, 1), (5, 2) and (2, 6). Count squares to estimate its area, then compute it exactly as half the absolute value of a 2 x 2 determinant of two edge vectors. For the example the exact area is 9.5.

quiz.q: A is 3 x 3 with det(A) = 5. You swap two rows and then multiply one row by 2. What is the new determinant?
quiz.explain: The swap gives -5, and scaling a row by 2 gives -10.

quiz.q: If A is 3 x 3 and det(A) = 2, what is det(3A)?
quiz.explain: det(kA) = k^n det(A) = 3^3 x 2 = 54.

quiz.q: Which statement is always true for square matrices A and B of the same size?
quiz.explain: The determinant is multiplicative: det(AB) = det(A) det(B). It does not split over addition.

quiz.q: Using Cramer's rule on x + y = 5, x - y = 1, what is x?
quiz.explain: det(A) = -1 - 1 = -2; replacing column 1 by b gives rows [5 1] and [1 -1], det = -5 - 1 = -6; x = -6 / -2 = 3.

quiz.q: What is the area of the parallelogram built on vectors (4, 1) and (2, 3)?

lessons.title: Vector Spaces and Subspaces
lessons.content:
Imagine a big playground with a strict rule at the gate: whatever you do inside, you are never allowed to walk out. You can run, you can jump, you can double your speed, you can turn around and go backwards, but you always stay inside the fence. A vector space is a mathematical playground like that. Inside it you are allowed two moves, adding things together and stretching them by a number, and no matter how you combine those moves, you never land outside. This lesson is about which playgrounds follow that rule, and how to check it quickly.

Why we need a bigger idea of vector: So far a vector has been an arrow or a list of numbers like (3, -1, 4). But lots of other things behave in exactly the same way. You can add two polynomials and get a polynomial. You can add two matrices of the same size and get a matrix. You can add two sound waves and get a sound wave. You can multiply any of them by 2 or by -0.5. If we write down the rules that lists of numbers obey and then prove theorems using only those rules, every theorem automatically works for polynomials, matrices, signals, images and anything else that obeys the same rules. That is the power of abstraction: prove once, use everywhere.

What a vector space is: A vector space is a set V of objects, called vectors, together with two operations. The first is addition, which takes two vectors u and v and gives a vector u + v. The second is scalar multiplication, which takes a real number c (a scalar) and a vector u and gives a vector cu. These operations must satisfy ten rules, called the axioms. They look long on paper, but each one is something you already believe about ordinary numbers.

The two closure axioms: Axiom 1 says that if u and v are in V, then u + v is also in V. Axiom 6 says that if u is in V and c is any real number, then cu is also in V. These are the fence rules of the playground. They are the ones that fail most often in exam questions, so always look at them first.

The addition axioms: Addition must be commutative, u + v = v + u, and associative, (u + v) + w = u + (v + w). There must be a zero vector 0 in V with u + 0 = u for every u. And every u must have a negative -u in V with u + (-u) = 0. Think of the zero vector as standing still and the negative as walking back exactly the way you came.

The scalar axioms: Scalar multiplication must play nicely with addition. c(u + v) = cu + cv, and (c + d)u = cu + du. Multiplying twice is like multiplying once by the product, c(du) = (cd)u. And multiplying by 1 changes nothing, 1u = u.

Example one, R^n: The set of all lists of n real numbers, with addition and scaling done entry by entry, is the standard example. For instance in R^3, (1, 2, 3) + (4, -2, 0) = (5, 0, 3) and 2(1, 2, 3) = (2, 4, 6). Every axiom holds because it holds for each entry, and entries are just real numbers. The zero vector is (0, 0, ..., 0) and the negative of (a, b, c) is (-a, -b, -c).

Example two, polynomials: Let P_n be the set of all polynomials of degree at most n. For P_2 that means everything of the form a + bx + cx^2, including things like 5 or 3x that have smaller degree. Add them by adding matching coefficients: (1 + 2x) + (3 - x + x^2) = 4 + x + x^2. Scale them by scaling every coefficient: 3(1 + 2x) = 3 + 6x. The zero vector is the zero polynomial, 0 + 0x + 0x^2. All ten axioms hold, so P_n is a vector space.

A tempting non-example: What about the polynomials of degree exactly 2? Take x^2 + x and -x^2. Both have degree exactly 2, but their sum is x, which has degree 1, so we walked out of the playground. The zero polynomial is also missing from that set. So "degree exactly 2" is not a vector space, while "degree at most 2" is. One small word changes the answer, and exam setters know it.

Example three, matrices: The set of all 2 x 2 matrices, written M_2x2, is a vector space with entry-by-entry addition and scaling, exactly as in the matrices lesson. The zero vector is the zero matrix. More generally, all m x n matrices form a vector space. Even the set of all real functions on an interval, like f(x) = sin x or g(x) = x^2, is a vector space if you define (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) and (cf)(x) = c f(x). The zero vector there is the function that is 0 everywhere.

More non-examples: The set of points (x, y) with x >= 0, the right half of the plane, is closed under addition, but multiply (1, 2) by -1 and you get (-1, -2), which is outside. So it fails scalar closure. The line y = x + 1 fails even faster: (0, 0) is not on it, so there is no zero vector. The unit circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 fails too, since (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) is not on the circle.

Small facts that follow from the axioms: Using only the ten rules you can prove that 0u = 0 (the number zero times any vector is the zero vector), c0 = 0, and (-1)u = -u. Here is the first proof, which is short and pretty. 0u = (0 + 0)u = 0u + 0u. Now add -(0u) to both sides, and you get 0 = 0u. Every step used only an axiom. This style of proof is exactly what exams ask in the "prove from the axioms" questions.

Subspaces: Very often we do not want a whole new space, just a piece of a space we already know. A subspace of V is a subset W of V that is itself a vector space using the same addition and scalar multiplication. For example, a plane through the origin sitting inside R^3 is a subspace. The good news is that you do not have to check all ten axioms again. Things like commutativity and associativity are inherited from V automatically, because W uses the same operations.

The subspace test: A subset W of V is a subspace if and only if three things hold. One, the zero vector of V is in W. Two, W is closed under addition: if u and v are in W, then u + v is in W. Three, W is closed under scalar multiplication: if u is in W and c is a scalar, then cu is in W. Checking zero first is a great trick, because if zero is missing you are done in one line.

Worked example, a plane: Let W be all (x, y, z) in R^3 with x + 2y - z = 0. Zero: 0 + 0 - 0 = 0, so (0, 0, 0) is in W. Addition: if u = (x1, y1, z1) and v = (x2, y2, z2) are in W, then (x1 + x2) + 2(y1 + y2) - (z1 + z2) = (x1 + 2y1 - z1) + (x2 + 2y2 - z2) = 0 + 0 = 0, so u + v is in W. Scaling: cx1 + 2cy1 - cz1 = c(x1 + 2y1 - z1) = c times 0 = 0, so cu is in W. All three hold, so W is a subspace. Notice that we used general letters, not specific numbers. Showing that it works for one or two examples proves nothing.

Worked example, a parabola: Let W be all (x, y) with y = x^2. Zero is in W, since 0 = 0^2. But (1, 1) is in W and 2(1, 1) = (2, 2) is not, because 2 is not 2^2 = 4. One counterexample is enough to say "not a subspace". So the rule is: to prove yes, use general symbols; to prove no, one specific counterexample is perfect.

Worked example, polynomials: In P_2, let W be all polynomials p with p(1) = 0. The zero polynomial gives 0 at x = 1, so it is in W. If p(1) = 0 and q(1) = 0 then (p + q)(1) = 0 + 0 = 0, and (cp)(1) = c times 0 = 0. So W is a subspace. For example x - 1 and x^2 - 1 are both in it. But the set with p(1) = 5 is not a subspace, since the zero polynomial gives 0, not 5.

All subspaces of R^2 and R^3: In R^2 there are only three kinds of subspaces: the single point {0}, lines through the origin, and the whole plane R^2. In R^3 there are four kinds: {0}, lines through the origin, planes through the origin, and all of R^3. The phrase "through the origin" is everything. A line that misses the origin, no matter how pretty, is not a subspace. These sizes, 0, 1, 2, 3, will be called dimensions in the basis and dimension lesson.

Where subspaces come from: The solution set of a homogeneous system Ax = 0 is always a subspace, because A0 = 0, A(u + v) = Au + Av = 0, and A(cu) = c(Au) = 0. This is the null space, a star of the four fundamental subspaces lesson. But the solution set of Ax = b with b not zero is never a subspace, since 0 is not a solution. The span of any set of vectors is also a subspace, which is the topic of the next lesson. The intersection of two subspaces is a subspace, but the union usually is not. The x-axis and y-axis are each subspaces of R^2, yet (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) is on neither, so their union fails.

Matrix subspaces: Inside M_2x2, the symmetric matrices (those with A^T = A) form a subspace, because the sum of two symmetric matrices is symmetric and a multiple of one is too. The upper triangular matrices form a subspace as well. But the invertible matrices do not: the zero matrix is not invertible, and I + (-I) = 0 shows that adding two invertible matrices can give a non-invertible one.

Real-life example one, photo editing: A grayscale photo of 100 x 100 pixels is a list of 10,000 brightness numbers, so it can be treated as a vector in R^10000. When an app blends two photos for a fade effect, it computes 0.7 times photo A plus 0.3 times photo B, which is just a linear combination. Making a picture darker is scalar multiplication. Real screens store pixel values between 0 and 255, which is not a subspace (multiply by -1 and you leave it), so apps clip values after the math. But the math in the middle is pure vector space work.

Real-life example two, sound and noise cancelling: Sound recorded by a phone is a function of time, and functions form a vector space. When a studio in Dhaka mixes a singer's voice with a tabla track, it adds two signals, maybe after scaling the volume of each.
