Noise-cancelling headphones use the additive inverse axiom in real life: a tiny microphone listens to the noise n, and the speaker plays roughly -n, so n + (-n) is close to the zero signal, which is silence. A bus horn on Mirpur Road becomes much quieter in your ears.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: The most common mistake is forgetting to check the zero vector. The second is proving closure with one numerical example instead of general symbols. The third is mixing up "at most degree n" with "exactly degree n". The fourth is thinking any line or plane is a subspace, when it must pass through the origin. Typical exam questions are: verify that P_n or M_mxn is a vector space; decide with reasons whether a given set like {(x, y, z) : x = 2y} or {(x, y) : xy >= 0} is a subspace; prove 0u = 0 from the axioms; and show that the solution set of Ax = 0 is a subspace.

Recap: A vector space is any set where adding and scaling keep you inside and the ten familiar rules hold. R^n, polynomials of degree at most n, m x n matrices and functions are all vector spaces. A subspace is a subset that is a vector space by itself, and the three-step test (zero, addition, scaling) decides it quickly. Next we look at span and linear independence, which tell us how a few vectors can build a whole subspace.
key_points: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication that satisfy ten axioms.
The closure axioms say that sums and scalar multiples never leave the set.
R^n, P_n (polynomials of degree at most n), m x n matrices and functions are vector spaces.
Polynomials of degree exactly 2 are not a vector space: sums can drop in degree and zero is missing.
Subspace test: contains 0, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiplication.
Subspaces of R^3 are {0}, lines through the origin, planes through the origin, and R^3.
Solutions of Ax = 0 form a subspace; solutions of Ax = b with b not 0 do not.
Intersections of subspaces are subspaces; unions usually are not.
lessons.tip: Always test the zero vector first. If it is missing, you can write 'not a subspace' in one line and move on.
lessons.task: On paper, write five sets of your own, for example {(x, y): y = 3x}, {(x, y): y = 3x + 1}, {(x, y): x >= 0}, symmetric 2x2 matrices, and polynomials with p(0) = 0. Run the three-step subspace test on each and give a counterexample for every one that fails.

quiz.q: Which of these is a subspace of R^2?
quiz.explain: y = 3x passes through the origin and is closed under addition and scaling. The others miss zero or break closure.

quiz.q: What is the quickest first check when testing a subspace?
options: Does it contain the zero vector?
quiz.explain: Every subspace must contain the zero vector, so if it is missing the answer is immediately no.

quiz.q: Why is the set of polynomials of degree exactly 2 not a vector space?
options: A sum can drop to lower degree and the zero polynomial is missing
quiz.explain: (x^2 + x) + (-x^2) = x has degree 1, and 0 is not of degree 2, so closure and the zero axiom fail.

quiz.q: Is the union of the x-axis and the y-axis a subspace of R^2?
options: No, because (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) is on neither axis
No, because it misses the zero vector
Yes, it equals all of R^2
quiz.explain: The union contains zero but is not closed under addition.

quiz.q: The solution set of Ax = b is a subspace exactly when:
options: A has more columns than rows
quiz.explain: A subspace must contain 0, and 0 solves Ax = b only when b = 0. For b = 0 the solution set is the null space.

lessons.title: Span and Linear Independence
lessons.content:
Imagine you have a box of paints with only red and yellow. By mixing them in different amounts you can make orange, a deep red-orange, a pale yellow-orange, and many more shades. Now a friend gives you a tube of ready-made orange. Does your palette get any richer? Not really, because you could already mix that orange yourself. The orange tube is redundant. This lesson is about exactly these two ideas: what you can build from a few vectors (span), and whether any of your vectors are redundant (linear dependence).

Linear combinations again: From the vectors lesson, a linear combination of vectors v1, v2, ..., vk is any vector of the form c1 v1 + c2 v2 + ... + ck vk, where c1, ..., ck are scalars, called the weights. For example, with v1 = (1, 2) and v2 = (1, 3), the combination 5v1 - v2 = (5, 10) - (1, 3) = (4, 7). Everything in this lesson is built on this one simple operation, so make sure you can compute combinations quickly and without mistakes.

What span means: The span of a set of vectors {v1, ..., vk}, written span{v1, ..., vk}, is the set of all their linear combinations, using every possible choice of weights. It is everything you can reach by stretching and adding those vectors. The span always contains the zero vector (choose all weights 0), and adding or scaling combinations gives another combination. So by the subspace test from the last lesson, a span is always a subspace. In fact it is the smallest subspace that contains all the vi.

Span in the plane: The span of a single nonzero vector like (1, 2) is the line through the origin in the direction of (1, 2), all points t(1, 2). The span of (1, 0) and (0, 1) is the whole plane R^2, because any (a, b) equals a(1, 0) + b(0, 1). But the span of (1, 2) and (2, 4) is still just the line, because (2, 4) is 2 times (1, 2) and points in the same direction. Two vectors give you a whole plane only if they point in genuinely different directions.

Span in space: In R^3, the span of two vectors that are not parallel, say (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 1), is a plane through the origin. To fill all of R^3 you need at least three vectors, and they must not all lie in one plane. For example (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1) span R^3. But (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (1, 1, 0) only span the flat xy-plane, because the third one lies in the plane of the first two.

Is b in the span: A very common question is whether a given vector b is in span{v1, ..., vk}. That means: are there weights with c1 v1 + ... + ck vk = b? Put the vi as the columns of a matrix A, and you are asking whether Ax = b has a solution. This is the column picture from the systems lesson. Example: is (4, 7) in span{(1, 2), (1, 3)}? Solve c1 + c2 = 4 and 2c1 + 3c2 = 7. Subtract twice the first from the second: c2 = 7 - 8 = -1, so c1 = 5. Check: 5(1, 2) + (-1)(1, 3) = (5 - 1, 10 - 3) = (4, 7). Yes, it is in the span.

A no example: Is (1, 2, 3) in span{(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)}? Any combination c1(1, 0, 0) + c2(0, 1, 0) = (c1, c2, 0) has third entry 0, but we need 3. So no weights work, the system is inconsistent, and (1, 2, 3) is not in the span. When you row reduce the augmented matrix in a no case, you get a row like 0 0 | 3, which says 0 = 3, impossible.

Spanning sets: We say a set S spans V (or is a spanning set for V) when span S = V, so every vector in V can be built. For R^n there is a clean test: put the vectors as columns of a matrix A and row reduce. The columns span R^n exactly when there is a pivot in every row. Then Ax = b is consistent for every b. If some row has no pivot, you can pick a b that leads to 0 = nonzero, and that b is unreachable. A useful consequence: fewer than n vectors can never span R^n, because a matrix with fewer than n columns cannot have n pivots.

Linear independence: A set of vectors {v1, ..., vk} is linearly independent if the only way to get c1 v1 + ... + ck vk = 0 is to take all weights equal to zero. That all-zero choice is called the trivial solution. If there is some other choice, with at least one weight not zero, that still gives the zero vector, the set is linearly dependent, and that choice is called a dependence relation.

What dependence really means: Dependence means at least one vector is a linear combination of the others, so it is redundant. Here is why. Suppose c1 v1 + c2 v2 + c3 v3 = 0 with c1 not zero. Divide by c1 and move things across: v1 = -(c2/c1) v2 - (c3/c1) v3. So v1 can be built from v2 and v3, and removing it would not shrink the span. Independence means no vector is a waste: each one adds a brand new direction. Like the orange paint tube, a dependent vector brings nothing new.

Quick rules to remember: A set containing the zero vector is always dependent, because 1 times 0 = 0 is a nontrivial relation. A single nonzero vector is independent. Two vectors are dependent exactly when one is a multiple of the other. And in R^n, any set of more than n vectors is automatically dependent, because a matrix with more columns than rows must have a free variable. So four vectors in R^3 can never be independent, no matter what they are.

Testing with row reduction: To test {v1, ..., vk} in R^n, put them as columns of A and solve Ac = 0. Row reduce A. If every column has a pivot, there are no free variables, the only solution is c = 0, and the set is independent. If some column has no pivot, that column's variable is free, you get nontrivial solutions, and the set is dependent. Notice the contrast with span: span needs a pivot in every row, independence needs a pivot in every column.

Worked example, dependent: Test v1 = (1, 2, 3), v2 = (4, 5, 6), v3 = (7, 8, 9). The matrix with these columns has rows (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 8), (3, 6, 9). Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives (0, -3, -6). Row 3 minus 3 times row 1 gives (0, -6, -12). Then row 3 minus 2 times the new row 2 gives (0, 0, 0). Only two pivots for three columns, so c3 is free and the set is dependent. To find the relation, set c3 = 1. From -3c2 - 6 = 0 we get c2 = -2. From c1 + 4(-2) + 7 = 0 we get c1 = 1. So v1 - 2v2 + v3 = 0. Check: (1 - 8 + 7, 2 - 10 + 8, 3 - 12 + 9) = (0, 0, 0). Indeed v2 is exactly halfway between v1 and v3.

Worked example, independent: Test (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1), (1, 1, 0). The matrix has rows (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1), (1, 1, 0). Row 3 minus row 1 gives (0, 1, -1). Row 3 minus row 2 gives (0, 0, -2). Three pivots in three columns, so the only solution is c = 0 and the set is independent. For n vectors in R^n there is also a shortcut from the determinant lessons: they are independent exactly when the determinant of the square matrix is not zero. Here det = 1(0 - 1) - 0 + 1(0 - 1) = -2, not zero, which agrees.

Independence beyond R^n: The same ideas work in any vector space. In P_2 the polynomials 1, x and x^2 are independent, because a + bx + cx^2 is the zero polynomial only when a = b = c = 0. But 1 + x, 1 - x and 2 are dependent, because (1 + x) + (1 - x) - 2 = 0. In M_2x2, the identity matrix and the matrix with all entries 1 are independent, since neither is a multiple of the other.

Span and independence together: Span asks whether you can reach everything. Independence asks whether there is any waste. In R^3, two vectors can be independent but can never span; four vectors can span but can never be independent. Exactly three vectors can do both, and then they span and are independent at the same time. A set that does both jobs is called a basis, which is the next lesson. Also note: if you remove a vector that is a combination of the others, the span stays the same. So any finite spanning set can be trimmed down until it becomes independent.

Real-life example one, fertilizer mixing: Suppose a farmer near Rajshahi has three fertilizer bags. To keep the numbers simple, say per kilogram bag A gives the nutrient vector (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) = (40, 0, 0) grams, bag B gives (0, 20, 10), and bag C gives (20, 10, 5). The farmer wants to know which nutrient mixes are possible. That is a span question. But check: C = 0.5A + 0.5B, since 0.5(40, 0, 0) + 0.5(0, 20, 10) = (20, 10, 5). So C is dependent on A and B; buying it adds no new possible mix. Also, because B always gives phosphorus and potassium in the ratio 2 to 1, a target like (40, 20, 20) is not in the span at all. A shop owner who understands this can advise the farmer to buy a bag that adds a genuinely new direction.

Real-life example two, data columns: A data scientist at a Dhaka e-commerce company has a table of products with columns for price in taka, price in US dollars, weight and rating. The dollar column is just the taka column times a fixed exchange rate, so those two columns, seen as vectors, are linearly dependent. Many machine learning models, such as linear regression, become unstable when columns are dependent, a problem called multicollinearity. The fix is to detect the dependence (row reduction or rank does it) and drop the redundant column. Same information, less confusion.

Common mistakes: Thinking that if no two vectors are parallel the set must be independent. Counterexample: (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1) are pairwise not parallel, but (1, 0) + (0, 1) - (1, 1) = 0, so they are dependent. Thinking that three vectors in R^3 always span R^3; they span only if they are independent. Confusing the span, which is a whole set (usually infinite), with the few vectors that generate it. Mixing up the pivot rules: every row for span, every column for independence. And forgetting that the zero vector makes any set dependent.

What exams ask: Determine whether a vector is in the span of others and find the weights. Decide whether given vectors span R^3. Test a set for linear independence and, if dependent, write one vector as a combination of the others. Find values of a parameter k that make a set dependent, which usually means setting a determinant equal to zero. And prove simple facts, like any set containing 0 is dependent, or a subset of an independent set is independent.

Recap: The span of some vectors is everything you can build from them with linear combinations, and it is always a subspace. Vectors are linearly independent when the only combination giving zero is the trivial one, which means none of them is redundant. Row reduction tests both: pivots in every row means spanning R^n, pivots in every column means independent. Next lesson we combine both ideas into a basis and use it to measure the size of a space, its dimension.
key_points: A linear combination is c1 v1 + ... + ck vk with scalar weights.
The span of a set is all its linear combinations, and it is always a subspace.
b is in span{v1, ..., vk} exactly when Ax = b is consistent, with the vi as columns of A.
Vectors are independent if only the trivial combination gives the zero vector.
Dependent means some vector is a combination of the others, so it is redundant.
Pivot in every row: columns span R^n. Pivot in every column: columns are independent.
More than n vectors in R^n are always dependent; fewer than n can never span R^n.
Any set containing the zero vector is dependent.
lessons.tip: Draw the vectors whenever you can. In R^2 and R^3, a quick sketch often tells you right away whether vectors are parallel or lie in one plane.
lessons.task: Pick three vectors in R^3 at random from your phone number digits, for example (0, 1, 7), (1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6). Put them as columns, row reduce on paper, and decide whether they are independent and whether they span R^3. If they are dependent, find the dependence relation and check it.

quiz.q: What is span{(1, 2), (2, 4)} in R^2?
options: A line that misses the origin
quiz.explain: (2, 4) = 2(1, 2), so all combinations are multiples of (1, 2), which form a line through the origin.

quiz.q: Which set is always linearly dependent?
options: Any set that contains the zero vector
quiz.explain: 1 times the zero vector plus 0 times the others gives 0, a nontrivial relation.

quiz.q: You have 4 vectors in R^3. What must be true?
quiz.explain: More vectors than entries means more columns than rows, so there is a free variable and a nontrivial relation.

quiz.q: Vectors placed as columns of A are independent exactly when:
options: The first entry of A is not zero
quiz.explain: A pivot in every column means no free variables, so Ac = 0 has only the trivial solution.

quiz.q: What about the set (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)?
options: Independent, because no two are parallel
Dependent, because it contains the zero vector
quiz.explain: Pairwise not parallel is not enough. (1, 0) + (0, 1) - (1, 1) = 0 is a nontrivial relation.

lessons.title: Basis and Dimension
lessons.content:
Imagine you are guiding a friend to a tea stall: "Walk 3 blocks east, then 2 blocks north." Two directions, east and north, and two numbers, 3 and 2, are enough to describe any spot in a neat grid of streets. You never need a third direction like northeast, because northeast is just a mix of east and north. And you cannot drop one of the two, because with only east you can never go north. That pair of directions is a basis, the number of directions you need is the dimension, and the numbers 3 and 2 are the coordinates. This lesson turns that everyday idea into precise math.

What a basis is: A basis of a vector space V is a set of vectors B = {b1, ..., bn} that does two jobs at once. It spans V, so every vector in V can be built from it. And it is linearly independent, so no vector in it is redundant. In the words of the last lesson: enough vectors to reach everything, and not a single one wasted. A basis is the smallest possible spanning set and, at the same time, the largest possible independent set.

The standard basis: In R^n the most obvious basis is e1 = (1, 0, ..., 0), e2 = (0, 1, 0, ..., 0), up to en = (0, ..., 0, 1). It spans, because (a1, ..., an) = a1 e1 + ... + an en, and it is independent, because that combination is zero only when every ai is zero. For example (3, -2, 5) = 3e1 - 2e2 + 5e3. The standard basis is so natural that we usually use it without noticing.

Other bases exist: A space has many bases, not just one. In R^2, take b1 = (1, 1) and b2 = (1, -1). They are not multiples of each other, so they are independent. Two independent vectors in R^2 also span it (we will see why below), so {(1, 1), (1, -1)} is a basis. So is {(2, 0), (0, 5)}, and so is {(1, 2), (3, 4)}. Choosing a clever basis is often the trick that makes a hard problem easy, which is the main idea of the change of basis and eigenvector lessons later.

Bases of other spaces: The standard basis of P_2 is {1, x, x^2}, since every a + bx + cx^2 is a combination of them and they are independent. The standard basis of P_n is {1, x, ..., x^n}. The standard basis of M_2x2 is the four matrices E11, E12, E21, E22, where Eij has a 1 in position (i, j) and 0 everywhere else. Any 2 x 2 matrix [a b; c d] equals a E11 + b E12 + c E21 + d E22.

Unique representation: Here is the reason bases are so useful. If B is a basis, every vector x in V can be written as a combination of the basis vectors in exactly one way. Spanning gives at least one way. For uniqueness, suppose x = c1 b1 + ... + cn bn and also x = d1 b1 + ... + dn bn. Subtract: 0 = (c1 - d1) b1 + ... + (cn - dn) bn. Independence says all these weights must be zero, so ci = di for every i. No two different recipes produce the same vector.

Dimension: A key theorem says that every basis of a given vector space has the same number of vectors. That shared number is called the dimension of V, written dim V. So dim R^n = n, dim P_n = n + 1 (count 1, x, ..., x^n), dim M_mxn = mn, and the zero space {0} has dimension 0, with the empty set as its basis. Some spaces, like the space of all polynomials, have no finite basis; we call them infinite-dimensional, but this course focuses on the finite ones.

Why all bases have the same size: The engine behind the theorem is this fact: if V is spanned by m vectors, then any set of more than m vectors in V is dependent. We already saw a version of it in R^n, where more than n vectors means more columns than rows and a free variable. Now take two bases, one with m vectors and one with k. The first spans and the second is independent, so k cannot be bigger than m. Swap roles and m cannot be bigger than k. So m = k. Dimension is a true property of the space, not of the basis you happened to pick.

Dimension of subspaces: Take the plane W = {(x, y, z) : x + 2y - z = 0} from the vector spaces lesson. Solve for x: x = -2y + z, with y and z free. Then (x, y, z) = (-2y + z, y, z) = y(-2, 1, 0) + z(1, 0, 1). The vectors (-2, 1, 0) and (1, 0, 1) span W and are not multiples of each other, so they form a basis, and dim W = 2. A plane through the origin in R^3 has dimension 2, a line through the origin has dimension 1, and {0} has dimension 0. The vectors have three entries, but the space they live in is only two-dimensional. The number of free variables told us the dimension.

Shortcuts when you know the dimension: Suppose dim V = n. Then any n linearly independent vectors in V automatically form a basis; you do not have to check spanning. And any n vectors that span V automatically form a basis; you do not have to check independence. Fewer than n vectors cannot span, and more than n cannot be independent. These shortcuts save a lot of time. For example, (1, 1) and (1, -1) are two independent vectors in a two-dimensional space, so they are a basis of R^2 with no extra work.

Shrinking a spanning set to a basis: If you have vectors that span a subspace but contain redundant ones, row reduce the matrix that has them as columns and keep the original vectors that sit in pivot columns. Take the vectors (1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6), (7, 8, 9) from the last lesson. Row reduction gave pivots in columns 1 and 2 only. So {(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)} is a basis for their span, and that span has dimension 2. Be careful to take the original columns, not the rows of the reduced matrix, because row operations change the column space.

Extending an independent set to a basis: Going the other way, you can add vectors to an independent set until it spans. Start with (1, 1, 0) in R^3. Add e2 = (0, 1, 0) and e3 = (0, 0, 1). The matrix with these columns has determinant 1(1 times 1 - 0 times 0) - 0 + 0 = 1, which is not zero, so the three are independent, and three independent vectors in R^3 form a basis. In general you keep adding standard basis vectors and throw away any that create dependence.

Coordinates relative to a basis: Since each vector has exactly one recipe in a basis B = {b1, ..., bn}, we can record the recipe. If x = c1 b1 + ... + cn bn, the coordinate vector of x relative to B is [x]_B = (c1, ..., cn). In the standard basis, coordinates are just the usual entries. In other bases they can look completely different, even though the vector itself has not moved at all. The order of the basis matters: list the vectors in a different order and the coordinates get shuffled.

Worked example, coordinates in R^2: Let B = {(1, 1), (1, -1)} and x = (5, 1). We want c1(1, 1) + c2(1, -1) = (5, 1), that is c1 + c2 = 5 and c1 - c2 = 1. Adding gives 2c1 = 6, so c1 = 3, and then c2 = 2. So [x]_B = (3, 2). Check: 3(1, 1) + 2(1, -1) = (3 + 2, 3 - 2) = (5, 1). Same arrow, new address: (5, 1) in the standard grid, (3, 2) in the tilted grid.

Coordinates as a matrix equation: Put the basis vectors as columns of a matrix P_B. Then x = P_B [x]_B. Because the columns form a basis, P_B is square and invertible, so [x]_B = P_B^-1 x. In the example, P_B = [1 1; 1 -1], and solving with it gave (3, 2). Moving between two different bases using such matrices is the topic of the change of basis lesson.

Worked example, coordinates for polynomials: In P_2 take the basis B = {1, 1 + x, 1 + x + x^2} and the polynomial p = 3 + 2x + x^2. Write p = a(1) + b(1 + x) + c(1 + x + x^2). Compare the x^2 terms: c = 1. Compare x terms: b + c = 2, so b = 1. Compare constants: a + b + c = 3, so a = 1. So [p]_B = (1, 1, 1). Check: 1 + (1 + x) + (1 + x + x^2) = 3 + 2x + x^2. Once you have coordinates, a polynomial becomes a list of three numbers, and every n-dimensional space can be handled exactly like R^n. That is why computers store a polynomial as an array of coefficients.

Real-life example one, colors in JPEG photos: A pixel color on screen is usually stored as (R, G, B), its coordinates in the red-green-blue basis. JPEG compression first converts colors into a different set of coordinates called YCbCr: Y is brightness and Cb and Cr describe color differences. It is the same color, just written in a different basis. Our eyes are much more sensitive to brightness detail than to color detail, so JPEG can store Cb and Cr with less detail and save space while the photo still looks good. Picking the right basis is what makes the saving possible.

Real-life example two, a delivery rider: Imagine a neighbourhood where the roads run diagonally to the north-east and north-west instead of along the compass. A foodpanda rider does not think "go 5 east and 1 north"; she thinks "go 3 blocks along the first road, then 2 blocks along the second". If one block along the first road is the vector (1, 1) and along the second is (1, -1), that is exactly our example: the address (5, 1) in compass coordinates becomes (3, 2) in road coordinates. Navigation apps convert between such coordinate systems all the time.

Common mistakes: Thinking a space has only one basis. It has many, but they all have the same size. Saying a plane in R^3 has dimension 3 because its vectors have three entries; it has dimension 2. Taking the pivot columns of the reduced matrix as a basis of the column space instead of the original columns. Forgetting that a basis must be independent, so a set with the zero vector is never a basis. Mixing up the order of basis vectors when writing coordinates. And claiming dim P_2 = 2, when it is 3 because of the constant term.

What exams ask: Show that a given set is a basis of R^3 or P_2. Find a basis and the dimension of a subspace described by an equation or by a span. Find the coordinates of a vector relative to a non-standard basis and check your answer. Extend an independent set to a basis, or reduce a spanning set to one. Prove that the representation in a basis is unique.

Recap: A basis is a set that spans and is independent. Every vector has exactly one set of coordinates in a basis. All bases of a space have the same size, and that size is the dimension: n for R^n, n + 1 for P_n, mn for m x n matrices. Coordinates let us treat any finite-dimensional space like R^n. Next we use these ideas to study the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix and the rank-nullity theorem.
key_points: A basis is a set of vectors that spans the space and is linearly independent.
The standard basis of R^n is e1, ..., en; of P_n it is 1, x, ..., x^n.
In a basis, every vector has exactly one set of coordinates.
All bases of a space have the same size; that number is the dimension.
dim R^n = n, dim P_n = n + 1, dim M_mxn = mn, dim {0} = 0.
In an n-dimensional space, n independent vectors or n spanning vectors are automatically a basis.
Keep the original pivot columns to shrink a spanning set to a basis.
Coordinates satisfy x = P_B [x]_B, so [x]_B = P_B^-1 x.
lessons.tip: Always check a basis answer by rebuilding the vector from its coordinates. One line of multiplication catches most mistakes.
lessons.task: On graph paper, draw the tilted grid made by (1, 1) and (1, -1). Mark three points like (5, 1), (2, 0) and (0, 4), and find their coordinates in the tilted grid both by counting on the paper and by solving equations. Check that both methods agree.

quiz.q: What is the dimension of P_3, the polynomials of degree at most 3?
quiz.explain: The basis is {1, x, x^2, x^3}, which has 4 vectors.

quiz.q: Which set is a basis of R^2?
quiz.explain: (1, 1) and (1, -1) are two independent vectors in a 2-dimensional space. The others are dependent or too few.

quiz.q: What are the coordinates of (5, 1) relative to the basis {(1, 1), (1, -1)}?
What is the dimension of the plane x + 2y - z = 0 in R^3?
quiz.explain: y and z are free, giving the basis (-2, 1, 0), (1, 0, 1), so the dimension is 2.

quiz.q: In a 4-dimensional space, you have 4 linearly independent vectors. Then they:
options: May fail to span the space
quiz.explain: When the number of independent vectors equals the dimension, they also span, so they form a basis.

lessons.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces
lessons.content:
Imagine a big building in Dhaka with four floors, and every floor has a different job. One floor holds everything the building can produce, one floor holds everything that gets thrown away, one floor holds the raw ingredients, and one floor holds the checks that catch mistakes. Every matrix A is like that building. It comes with four special sets of vectors, called the four fundamental subspaces, and once you know them you understand almost everything about what A can and cannot do. This lesson ties together span, independence, basis and dimension from the last few lessons into one clean picture.

The setup: Let A be an m x n matrix, meaning m rows and n columns. When we multiply A by a vector x, the vector x must have n entries, so x lives in R^n. The answer Ax has m entries, so it lives in R^m. Keep these two spaces apart in your head. Two of the four subspaces live in R^n (the input side) and two live in R^m (the output side). Mixing them up is the single most common mistake students make in this topic.

The four names: The column space C(A) is the span of the columns of A, and it lives in R^m. The null space N(A) is the set of all x with Ax = 0, and it lives in R^n. The row space C(A^T) is the span of the rows of A, and it lives in R^n. The left null space N(A^T) is the set of all y with A^T y = 0, and it lives in R^m. The left null space gets its name because A^T y = 0 is the same as y^T A = 0, where y sits on the left of A.

Our example matrix: We will use one matrix all the way through. Let A have rows (1, 2, 1), (2, 4, 3) and (3, 6, 4). So A is 3 x 3. Row reduce it. Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives (0, 0, 1). Row 3 minus 3 times row 1 gives (0, 0, 1). Row 3 minus the new row 2 gives (0, 0, 0). Finally row 1 minus row 2 gives (1, 2, 0). The reduced row echelon form R has rows (1, 2, 0), (0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 0). The pivots are in column 1 and column 3, and column 2 has no pivot.

Rank: The rank r of A is the number of pivots. For our A, r = 2. Rank is the most important single number about a matrix. It tells you how many truly independent columns A has, and also how many truly independent rows. Here column 2, which is (2, 4, 6), is just 2 times column 1, so it adds nothing new. And row 3 is row 1 plus row 2, so it adds nothing new either. Two independent directions, so rank 2.

The column space: C(A) is everything you can get as Ax, so it is the set of all outputs the matrix can produce. A basis is the columns of the ORIGINAL A that sit in pivot positions. For us that is column 1 = (1, 2, 3) and column 3 = (1, 3, 4). So C(A) is a plane through the origin inside R^3, and its dimension is r = 2. Careful: do not take the columns of R as the basis. Row operations change the column space. Column 1 of R is (1, 0, 0), which is not even in C(A).

What the column space tells you: The equation Ax = b has a solution exactly when b is in the column space. For our A you can check that every column satisfies y1 + y2 - y3 = 0: 1 + 2 - 3 = 0, 2 + 4 - 6 = 0, 1 + 3 - 4 = 0. So every output b must satisfy b1 + b2 = b3. The vector b = (1, 1, 2) passes this test, and indeed x = (2, 0, -1) solves Ax = b. The vector b = (1, 1, 1) fails, and no x at all can produce it.

The null space: N(A) is every x that the matrix squashes to zero. To find it, solve Rx = 0, because row operations do not change the solutions. The rows of R say x1 + 2 x2 = 0 and x3 = 0. The free variable is x2, so set x2 = t. Then x1 = -2t and x3 = 0, so x = t(-2, 1, 0). A basis of N(A) is the single vector (-2, 1, 0). Check: A times (-2, 1, 0) gives (-2 + 2, -4 + 4, -6 + 6) = (0, 0, 0). The dimension of the null space, called the nullity, is the number of free variables, here 1.

Why the null space matters: If x_p is one solution of Ax = b, then every solution is x_p plus something from the null space. For b = (1, 1, 2), the complete solution is x = (2, 0, -1) + t(-2, 1, 0). If N(A) contains only the zero vector, solutions are unique whenever they exist. If N(A) is bigger, you get infinitely many solutions whenever you get one. So the null space measures how much freedom, or how much ambiguity, the system has.

The row space: C(A^T) is the span of the rows. Here is a happy fact: row operations do not change the row space, because each new row is a combination of the old ones and the steps can be undone. So the nonzero rows of R form a basis: (1, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 1). The row space is a plane in R^3, and its dimension is again r = 2. For the row space you may use the rows of R; for the column space you must go back to A. Write that difference on your hand before the exam.

The left null space: N(A^T) holds every y with y^T A = 0, in other words every combination of the rows that cancels to zero. We already spotted that row 1 + row 2 - row 3 = 0, so y = (1, 1, -1) is in the left null space. Its dimension is m - r = 3 - 2 = 1, so (1, 1, -1) is a basis. Notice that this is exactly the test vector we used for the column space: b is reachable exactly when y^T b = 0, meaning b1 + b2 - b3 = 0. The left null space gives you the conditions that every reachable output must obey.

The dimension count: Putting it together, for any m x n matrix of rank r: dim C(A) = r, dim C(A^T) = r, dim N(A) = n - r, and dim N(A^T) = m - r. On the input side, row space plus null space dimensions add to r + (n - r) = n. On the output side, column space plus left null space add to r + (m - r) = m. Nothing is lost and nothing is double counted.

The rank-nullity theorem: The input-side count is famous enough to get its own name. For any m x n matrix, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of columns. In words: every column is either a pivot column (contributing to rank) or a free column (contributing to the null space). For our A: 2 + 1 = 3. A quick use: a 5 x 8 matrix has rank at most 5, so its null space has dimension at least 8 - 5 = 3. That instantly tells you Ax = 0 has infinitely many solutions without any row reduction.

Row rank equals column rank: It is surprising at first that the number of independent rows always equals the number of independent columns, even for a long thin matrix like 2 x 100. The reason is that both are counted by the same pivots. That is why we can talk about one number, the rank, and why rank(A) = rank(A^T). It also gives the bound rank(A) <= min(m, n).

The orthogonality picture: Here is the beautiful part. Every vector in the null space is perpendicular to every vector in the row space. Why? Ax = 0 says each row of A dotted with x gives 0. Check with our numbers: (-2, 1, 0) dotted with (1, 2, 0) is -2 + 2 + 0 = 0, and dotted with (0, 0, 1) is 0. In the same way, the left null space is perpendicular to the column space: (1, 1, -1) dotted with (1, 2, 3) is 0. So R^n splits into two perpendicular pieces, row space and null space, and R^m splits into column space and left null space. The orthogonality lesson later builds on this.

Full rank cases: If r = n (full column rank), the null space is just {0}, the columns are independent, and Ax = b has at most one solution. If r = m (full row rank), the column space is all of R^m, the left null space is {0}, and Ax = b has at least one solution for every b. If r = m = n, the matrix is square and invertible, and Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b. This lines up neatly with the invertible matrix theorem from the inverse lesson.

Real life example 1, a marks spreadsheet: Suppose a teacher in a Chattogram school keeps a table with one row per student and columns for Bangla, English, Math and Total. The Total column is Bangla + English + Math, so it is a combination of the other columns. The rank of this 40 x 4 matrix is at most 3, not 4. The vector (1, 1, 1, -1) is in the null space, because Bangla + English + Math - Total = 0 for every student. Data scientists hunt for exactly this kind of hidden dependency, because duplicated information can confuse machine learning models and waste storage. Rank tells you how many columns carry genuinely new information.

Real life example 2, a road network: Think of four bus stops in Dhaka joined by five roads. Build an incidence matrix with one row per road and one column per stop: put -1 where the road starts and +1 where it ends. If x holds a height (or electrical potential) at each stop, then Ax gives the differences along each road. The null space is the constant vectors, like (1, 1, 1, 1), because if every stop has the same height, every difference is zero. So for a connected network the rank is 4 - 1 = 3. The left null space has dimension 5 - 3 = 2, and its vectors are flows around closed loops of roads. This is exactly how Kirchhoff's laws for electric circuits are written in linear algebra, and network engineers use it every day.

Common mistakes: Taking the columns of R instead of A as the column space basis. Forgetting which space each subspace lives in: for a 3 x 5 matrix, the null space is in R^5, not R^3. Writing nullity = m - r instead of n - r. Thinking a basis vector of the null space must have a 1 in it; any nonzero multiple works. And claiming a set of vectors is a subspace when it does not contain zero, which can never happen for these four, since each is a span or a solution set of a homogeneous system.

What exams ask: Find bases and dimensions of all four subspaces of a given 3 x 4 matrix. Use rank-nullity to find the nullity without solving. Decide whether a given b is in the column space. Show that a null space vector is orthogonal to the rows. Explain what full column rank means for uniqueness of solutions. Practise one full example by hand, check every basis vector by multiplying, and these questions become routine marks.

Recap: Every m x n matrix of rank r has four subspaces. Column space (outputs, in R^m, dimension r), null space (inputs killed by A, in R^n, dimension n - r), row space (in R^n, dimension r) and left null space (in R^m, dimension m - r). Rank plus nullity equals n. Row space is perpendicular to null space, and column space is perpendicular to left null space. With this map in your head, every question about solving Ax = b becomes a question about which floor of the building you are standing on.
key_points: An m x n matrix has four subspaces: column space and left null space in R^m, row space and null space in R^n.
Rank r = number of pivots = dim of column space = dim of row space, and rank(A) = rank(A^T).
A column space basis uses the ORIGINAL columns of A in pivot positions; a row space basis can use the nonzero rows of the echelon form.
The null space is found by solving Rx = 0; its dimension (nullity) is the number of free variables, n - r.
Rank-nullity theorem: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of columns.
The left null space has dimension m - r and gives the conditions b must satisfy for Ax = b to be solvable.
Row space is perpendicular to null space; column space is perpendicular to left null space.
lessons.tip: Make a small 2 x 2 table on one page with the four subspace names, the space each lives in, its dimension and how to find a basis. Redo it from memory once a day for a week and this whole topic becomes automatic.
lessons.task: Take the matrix with rows (1, 1, 2) and (2, 2, 4). By hand, find its rank, a basis for each of the four subspaces, and check that rank + nullity = 3. Then verify one null space vector is perpendicular to the first row by computing the dot product.

quiz.q: For a 4 x 7 matrix A, where does the null space N(A) live?
quiz.explain: Ax = 0 needs x to have 7 entries (one per column), so N(A) is a subspace of R^7.

quiz.q: A 5 x 8 matrix has rank 3. What is the dimension of its null space?
quiz.explain: Rank-nullity: nullity = n - r = 8 - 3 = 5.

quiz.q: After row reducing A to R, which statement is correct?
options: The nonzero rows of R are a basis for the row space of A
The pivot columns of R are a basis for the column space of A
Row operations change the null space
Row operations change the row space
quiz.explain: Row operations keep the row space and null space but change the column space, so use A's original pivot columns for the column space.

quiz.q: For a 3 x 3 matrix of rank 2, what is the dimension of the left null space N(A^T)?
quiz.explain: dim N(A^T) = m - r = 3 - 2 = 1.

quiz.q: Every vector in the null space of A is perpendicular to every vector in which subspace?
quiz.explain: Ax = 0 means each row dotted with x is zero, so null space vectors are orthogonal to the whole row space.

lessons.title: Linear Transformations
lessons.content:
Think of a juice machine at a shop in New Market. You put fruit in, juice comes out. Now imagine a very well-behaved machine: if you put in twice as much fruit, you get exactly twice as much juice, and if you put in mangoes and oranges together, you get exactly the mango juice plus the orange juice you would have got separately. A machine that respects adding and scaling like that is what mathematicians call a linear transformation. Matrices, it turns out, are just a neat way to write such machines down.

What a transformation is: A transformation (also called a map or function) T from a vector space V to a vector space W takes each vector v in V and gives back a vector T(v) in W. V is called the domain and W the codomain. For example, T(x, y) = (2x, x + y) takes vectors from R^2 and returns vectors in R^2. So far this is just a function, like the ones you met in school, except the inputs and outputs are vectors.

The definition of linear: T is linear if two rules hold for all vectors u, v and every scalar c. Rule one, additivity: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v). Rule two, homogeneity: T(c v) = c T(v). You can combine them into one test: T(a u + b v) = a T(u) + b T(v). In words, a linear map sends combinations to combinations. Whatever recipe you used to mix the inputs, the outputs get mixed with the same recipe.

Checking an example: Take T(x, y) = (2x, x + y). Let u = (x1, y1) and v = (x2, y2). Then T(u + v) = (2(x1 + x2), (x1 + x2) + (y1 + y2)) = (2x1, x1 + y1) + (2x2, x2 + y2) = T(u) + T(v). And T(c u) = (2c x1, c x1 + c y1) = c(2 x1, x1 + y1) = c T(u). Both rules hold, so T is linear.

Two non-examples: Take S(x, y) = (x + 1, y). Then S(0, 0) = (1, 0), not (0, 0). But every linear map must send zero to zero, because T(0) = T(0 times v) = 0 times T(v) = 0. So S is not linear. It is a shift, and we will see in the next lesson how graphics handles shifts with a trick. Now take Q(x, y) = (x y, y). Then Q(2, 2) = (4, 2), but 2 times Q(1, 1) = 2 times (1, 1) = (2, 2). Scaling fails, so Q is not linear either. Products of variables, squares, constants added on, sines and absolute values all break linearity.

The quick zero test: Before doing any algebra, compute T(0). If it is not zero, the map is not linear and you are done. If it is zero, you still have to check the two rules, because passing the zero test alone does not prove linearity. Q above passes the zero test (Q(0, 0) = (0, 0)) but is still not linear.

Every matrix gives a linear map: If A is an m x n matrix, then T(x) = Ax is a linear map from R^n to R^m. This is because matrix multiplication already obeys A(u + v) = Au + Av and A(c u) = c Au. So every matrix you have met in this course is secretly a machine that transforms vectors.

Every linear map on R^n is a matrix: The reverse is the magical part. If T from R^n to R^m is linear, there is exactly one matrix A with T(x) = Ax for every x. To build it, feed in the standard basis vectors e1, e2, ..., en and record the outputs as columns: A = [T(e1) T(e2) ... T(en)]. This works because any x = x1 e1 + ... + xn en, so by linearity T(x) = x1 T(e1) + ... + xn T(en), which is exactly A times x written as a combination of columns. This A is called the standard matrix of T.

Building a standard matrix: Let T(x, y) = (x + 2y, 3x, y - x), a map from R^2 to R^3. Then T(e1) = T(1, 0) = (1, 3, -1) and T(e2) = T(0, 1) = (2, 0, 1). So A is the 3 x 2 matrix with rows (1, 2), (3, 0) and (-1, 1). Check with x = (4, 5): the formula gives (4 + 10, 12, 5 - 4) = (14, 12, 1), and A times (4, 5) gives (4 + 10, 12 + 0, -4 + 5) = (14, 12, 1). They match.

Maps between other vector spaces: Linear maps are not limited to R^n. Differentiation is linear: the derivative of (f + g) is f' + g', and the derivative of c f is c f'. Take D from P2 (polynomials of degree at most 2) to P1, with D(a + b x + c x^2) = b + 2c x. Using the basis {1, x, x^2} for P2 and {1, x} for P1, the images are D(1) = 0, D(x) = 1 and D(x^2) = 2x. Their coordinate vectors are (0, 0), (1, 0) and (0, 2), so the matrix of D is the 2 x 3 matrix with rows (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 2). Any linear map between finite-dimensional spaces can be written as a matrix once you choose bases. The change of basis lesson digs into how that matrix changes when the bases change.

Kernel: The kernel of T, written ker(T), is the set of all v in the domain with T(v) = 0. For T(x) = Ax, the kernel is exactly the null space N(A) from the last lesson. It is always a subspace of the domain. For D on polynomials, the kernel is the constant polynomials, because the derivative of a constant is 0.

Range: The range (or image) of T is the set of all outputs T(v). For T(x) = Ax, the range is exactly the column space C(A). It is always a subspace of the codomain. For the 3 x 2 matrix above, the range is the plane in R^3 spanned by (1, 3, -1) and (2, 0, 1).

Rank-nullity again: For a linear map from an n-dimensional space, dim ker(T) + dim range(T) = n. This is the same theorem as rank + nullity = number of columns, just dressed in transformation clothes. For D from P2 (dimension 3) to P1: the kernel has dimension 1 (constants) and the range is all of P1 (dimension 2), and 1 + 2 = 3. Good.

One-to-one: T is one-to-one (injective) if different inputs always give different outputs. Here is the key fact: a linear T is one-to-one exactly when ker(T) = {0}. Why? If T(u) = T(v) then T(u - v) = 0, so u - v is in the kernel. If the kernel is only zero, then u = v. For a matrix map, one-to-one means the columns are independent, which means rank = n. Our 3 x 2 example has independent columns, so it is one-to-one.

Onto: T is onto (surjective) if every vector in the codomain is hit by some input, which means range(T) = W. For a matrix map from R^n to R^m, onto means the column space is all of R^m, which means rank = m. Our 3 x 2 example has rank 2, which is less than 3, so it is not onto. Its outputs fill only a plane inside R^3. In general a map from R^2 to R^3 can never be onto, and a map from R^3 to R^2 can never be one-to-one, simply by counting dimensions.

The square case: When the domain and codomain have the same dimension n, one-to-one and onto become the same thing. Either both hold or neither does, and when both hold T is invertible, with inverse map given by the inverse matrix. Example: the projection P(x, y, z) = (x, y, 0) from R^3 to R^3 has kernel equal to the z-axis and range equal to the xy-plane. It is neither one-to-one nor onto, and its matrix has determinant 0.

Composition is multiplication: If T(x) = Ax and S(y) = By, then doing T first and then S gives S(T(x)) = B(Ax) = (BA)x. So the matrix of the combined machine is BA, with the first map written on the right. This explains why matrix multiplication is defined the strange row-times-column way: it was designed so that multiplying matrices means chaining transformations. It also explains why AB and BA differ, because doing things in a different order usually gives a different result.

Real life example 1, turning colour into grey: A phone photo stores each pixel as (R, G, B). A common way to make it black and white is gray = 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B. That is a linear map from R^3 to R^1, with a 1 x 3 matrix (0.299, 0.587, 0.114). Its kernel is a 2-dimensional plane of colour vectors that give zero (every nonzero one has a negative entry, so none of them is a real colour), and it is onto R^1 but not one-to-one: many different colours become the same grey. That is why you cannot perfectly recover the colours from a grey photo.

Real life example 2, an online order: Suppose a Daraz seller sells pens for 10 taka, notebooks for 50 taka and bags for 800 taka. The bill for an order (p, n, b) is 10p + 50n + 800b, a linear map from R^3 to R^1. Double the order, double the bill. Now add a fixed 60 taka delivery charge. The new bill 10p + 50n + 800b + 60 is not linear any more, because an empty order costs 60, not 0. Maps like this, linear plus a constant, are called affine. Neural network layers compute W x + b, which is also affine: a linear part W x plus a shift b.

Common mistakes: Thinking a straight-line formula like f(x) = 3x + 5 is linear in this sense; it is affine, because f(0) = 5. Writing the composed matrix as AB when T is applied first; it should be BA. Building the standard matrix with T(e_i) as rows instead of columns. And confusing one-to-one with onto: one-to-one is about the kernel being {0}, onto is about the range filling the whole codomain.

What exams ask: Prove or disprove that a given map is linear. Find the standard matrix from a formula or from the images of e1 and e2. Find the kernel and range and their dimensions. Decide whether T is one-to-one or onto, with a reason based on rank. Find the matrix of a composition. Write the matrix of differentiation or of a simple map on polynomials relative to given bases.

Recap: A linear transformation respects addition and scaling, so it always sends 0 to 0 and combinations to combinations. Every linear map between R^n and R^m is multiplication by a matrix whose columns are T(e1), ..., T(en). The kernel is the null space, the range is the column space, and their dimensions add up to the domain dimension. One-to-one means a zero kernel, onto means a full range, and chaining maps means multiplying matrices in reverse order. Next lesson we put these ideas to work moving shapes around a screen.
key_points: T is linear when T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(c v) = c T(v) for all vectors and scalars.
Every linear map sends 0 to 0; if T(0) is not 0 the map is not linear, but passing this test alone proves nothing.
The standard matrix of T from R^n to R^m has columns T(e1), T(e2), ..., T(en).
Kernel = all inputs sent to 0 (the null space); range = all outputs (the column space).
dim ker(T) + dim range(T) = dimension of the domain (rank-nullity).
One-to-one exactly when the kernel is {0} (rank = n); onto exactly when the range is the whole codomain (rank = m).
Doing T(x) = Ax first and then S(y) = By has matrix BA; maps like x -> Ax + b are affine, not linear.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet a new map, first compute T(0), then T(e1) and T(e2). In ten seconds you know whether it can be linear and, if it is, you already have its matrix.
lessons.task: Write the standard matrix of T(x, y) = (3x - y, x + 4y). Pick any two vectors u and v on paper and check that T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) using the matrix. Then decide whether T is one-to-one by checking whether its columns are independent.

quiz.q: Which map from R^2 to R^2 is linear?
quiz.explain: Only (2x - y, 3y) has every output entry a plain combination of x and y with no constants, products or powers.

quiz.q: T(1, 0) = (2, 5) and T(0, 1) = (-1, 3). What is the standard matrix of T?
quiz.explain: T(e1) and T(e2) become the columns, so the columns are (2, 5) and (-1, 3), giving rows (2, -1) and (5, 3).

quiz.q: For T(x) = Ax, the kernel of T is the same as which subspace of A?
quiz.explain: The kernel is all x with Ax = 0, which is exactly the null space N(A).

quiz.q: A linear map T from R^5 to R^3 has rank 3. Which is true?
options: T is onto but not one-to-one
quiz.explain: Rank 3 = m means onto; the kernel has dimension 5 - 3 = 2, so it is not one-to-one.

quiz.q: You apply T(x) = Ax first and then S(y) = By. What is the matrix of the combined map?
quiz.explain: S(T(x)) = B(Ax) = (BA)x, so the map applied first sits on the right.

lessons.title: Geometric Transformations for Graphics
lessons.content:
Open any game on your phone, pinch to zoom on a photo, or watch the map in a ride-sharing app spin as the rider turns a corner. Every one of those moves, stretching, turning, flipping, sliding, is done by multiplying the coordinates of points by small matrices, millions of times per second. In this lesson you will learn the exact matrices that do these jobs, how to chain them, and the clever trick that lets even sliding (translation) become a matrix multiplication.

The big idea: A picture on a screen is made of points, and each point is a vector (x, y). A shape like a triangle is stored as its corner points. To move the whole shape, you do not redraw it by hand; you multiply each corner by the same matrix and join the new corners. Because the map is linear, straight lines stay straight lines and the origin stays put. All you need is to know where the matrix sends e1 = (1, 0) and e2 = (0, 1), since those images are the columns, as we saw in the last lesson.

Scaling: The matrix with rows (sx, 0) and (0, sy) sends (x, y) to (sx x, sy y). It stretches horizontally by sx and vertically by sy. If sx = sy = 2, everything doubles in size, like zooming in. If sx = 3 and sy = 1, shapes get wider but not taller. Example: the triangle with corners (0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1) has area 1. Scale with sx = 3, sy = 2 and the corners become (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 2), with area 6. The determinant of the scaling matrix is 3 times 2 = 6, and that is exactly the area factor, just as the determinant lesson promised.

Rotation: To rotate every point counterclockwise about the origin by an angle theta, use the matrix with rows (cos theta, -sin theta) and (sin theta, cos theta). Why these numbers? Rotating e1 = (1, 0) by theta lands on (cos theta, sin theta), which is the first column. Rotating e2 = (0, 1) lands on (-sin theta, cos theta), the second column. For theta = 90 degrees, cos = 0 and sin = 1, so the matrix has rows (0, -1) and (1, 0), and (3, 2) goes to (-2, 3). For theta = 30 degrees, cos is about 0.866 and sin is 0.5, so (2, 0) goes to about (1.732, 1).

Facts about rotations: A rotation matrix has determinant cos^2 + sin^2 = 1, so it never changes area. Its columns are perpendicular unit vectors, so it is an orthogonal matrix, and its inverse is its transpose, which is the same as rotating by minus theta. Rotating by alpha and then by beta is the same as rotating by alpha + beta, and in 2D the order does not matter for two rotations about the same point. To rotate clockwise, just use a negative angle.

Reflection: A reflection flips the plane over a mirror line through the origin. Across the x-axis: rows (1, 0) and (0, -1), sending (x, y) to (x, -y). Across the y-axis: rows (-1, 0) and (0, 1), sending (x, y) to (-x, y). Across the line y = x: rows (0, 1) and (1, 0), which swaps x and y, so (3, 1) goes to (1, 3). Every reflection has determinant -1. The minus sign means orientation flips: a shape traced counterclockwise comes out traced clockwise, like your right hand looking like a left hand in a mirror. Reflecting twice across the same line gives back the original, so a reflection matrix is its own inverse.

Shear: A horizontal shear with factor k has rows (1, k) and (0, 1), sending (x, y) to (x + k y, y). Points slide sideways by an amount proportional to their height, like pushing the top of a stack of books while the bottom stays put. With k = 1, the unit square with corners (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1) becomes the parallelogram (0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 1). The determinant is 1, so the area stays 1 even though the shape tilts. Italic text on a screen is basically a small shear of normal letters. A vertical shear has rows (1, 0) and (k, 1).

Projection: The matrix with rows (1, 0) and (0, 0) sends (x, y) to (x, 0), squashing everything flat onto the x-axis. Its determinant is 0, which tells you area is destroyed and the map cannot be undone. You lose the y information forever. Projections are how 3D scenes are flattened onto a 2D screen, though real cameras use a perspective version described below.

Composition: To do several moves in a row, multiply the matrices, with the first move on the right. If you rotate with R and then scale with S, the combined matrix is S R, and a point p goes to S R p. The order matters a lot. Let R be the 90 degree rotation, rows (0, -1) and (1, 0), and F the reflection across the x-axis, rows (1, 0) and (0, -1). Rotate first, then reflect: F R has rows (0, -1) and (-1, 0). Reflect first, then rotate: R F has rows (0, 1) and (1, 0). Try the point (1, 0). Rotating gives (0, 1), then reflecting gives (0, -1). But reflecting first leaves (1, 0) alone, and rotating then gives (0, 1). Two different answers, so FR is not RF.

Why games love composition: A game might need to scale a character, rotate it, and then do the same for its weapon relative to the hand. Instead of applying five matrices to each of thousands of points, the program multiplies the five matrices together once, getting a single combined matrix, and then applies that one matrix to every point. One small matrix product saves a huge amount of work. This is a big reason GPUs are built to do matrix multiplication extremely fast.

The problem with translation: Sliding a shape by (tx, ty), so (x, y) goes to (x + tx, y + ty), is the most basic move of all. But it is not linear, because it moves the origin: (0, 0) goes to (tx, ty). No 2 x 2 matrix can do it, since any matrix times (0, 0) is (0, 0). That would be a disaster for graphics, where we want every move to be one matrix in one long chain.

Homogeneous coordinates, the trick: Write each 2D point (x, y) as a 3D vector (x, y, 1), adding a 1 at the end. Now use 3 x 3 matrices. The translation matrix has rows (1, 0, tx), (0, 1, ty) and (0, 0, 1). Multiply by (x, y, 1) and you get (x + tx, y + ty, 1). The extra 1 picks up the shift. Example: translate (2, 3) by (5, -1). The product is (2 + 5, 3 - 1, 1) = (7, 2, 1), so the new point is (7, 2). Geometrically we are doing a shear in 3D on the plane z = 1, which looks like a slide when you only look at that plane.

The old moves in the new clothes: Any 2 x 2 matrix M fits into homogeneous form by putting M in the top-left corner, zeros in the rest of the last column and bottom row, and a 1 in the bottom-right corner. So rotation becomes rows (cos, -sin, 0), (sin, cos, 0), (0, 0, 1). Now rotations, scalings, reflections, shears and translations are all 3 x 3 matrices and can be multiplied into one combined matrix.

Rotating around a point that is not the origin: Suppose you want to rotate the point (3, 1) by 90 degrees around the centre c = (2, 1), like spinning a wheel that is not at the origin. The recipe is: translate so that c moves to the origin, rotate, then translate back. In matrix form that is T(c) R T(-c), applied right to left. Step by step: (3, 1) minus (2, 1) is (1, 0). Rotating (1, 0) by 90 degrees gives (0, 1). Adding (2, 1) back gives (2, 2). So (3, 1) goes to (2, 2). Check: the distance from the centre is 1 before and after, and the direction turned from pointing right to pointing up. Exams love this question.

Going to 3D: In 3D, points are (x, y, z) and homogeneous points are (x, y, z, 1), so graphics engines use 4 x 4 matrices. Rotation about the z-axis by theta has the 2D rotation in its top-left 2 x 2 block and leaves z unchanged: rows (cos, -sin, 0), (sin, cos, 0), (0, 0, 1) in 3D. Rotations about x and y look similar with the roles swapped. Systems like OpenGL, DirectX, Unity and Unreal multiply a model matrix (placing the object in the world), a view matrix (placing the camera) and a projection matrix (making far things look smaller) into one matrix, then apply it to every vertex. For perspective, the projection matrix puts depth information into the fourth coordinate w, and the hardware divides x and y by w at the end, which is why distant objects shrink.

Real life example 1, editing a photo on your phone: When you rotate a photo by 90 degrees in your gallery app, each pixel position (x, y) is mapped by a rotation and a translation so the image stays on screen. When you pinch to zoom, a scaling about the point between your fingers is used, which is translate, scale, translate back, exactly like rotating around a point. Flipping a selfie so that the text reads correctly is a reflection across the vertical axis. All of it is 3 x 3 homogeneous matrices.

Real life example 2, a map in a ride app: When a rider in Dhaka uses a ride or delivery app in navigation mode, the map rotates so that the direction of travel always points up. The app takes map coordinates, translates so the rider's position is at the centre, rotates by minus the heading angle, scales according to the zoom level, and translates to the middle of the screen. Four matrices, multiplied into one, are applied to every road and building point each time the phone's compass updates.

Common mistakes: Writing the rotation matrix with the minus sign in the wrong place; check by rotating (1, 0) by 90 degrees, which must give (0, 1). Multiplying in the wrong order: the first transformation goes on the right. Trying to do translation with a 2 x 2 matrix. Forgetting to translate back after translating to the origin. Mixing degrees and radians when computing sine and cosine on a calculator.

What exams ask: Write the matrix for a given rotation, reflection, scaling or shear. Find the image of a triangle under a combination of moves and draw it. Show that two transformations do not commute. Use the determinant to say how area changes and whether orientation flips. Write the 3 x 3 homogeneous matrix for translation, or for rotation about a given point, and apply it.

Recap: Scaling, rotation, reflection, shear and projection are all linear and have 2 x 2 matrices built from the images of e1 and e2. Determinants tell the area factor: rotation 1, reflection -1, shear 1, scaling sx times sy, projection 0. Composition is multiplication with the first move on the right, and order matters. Translation is not linear, but homogeneous coordinates turn it into a 3 x 3 (or 4 x 4 in 3D) matrix, so that every move in computer graphics becomes one matrix in one chain.
key_points: Scaling: rows (sx, 0), (0, sy); determinant sx times sy is the area factor.
Counterclockwise rotation by theta: rows (cos, -sin), (sin, cos); determinant 1 and inverse = transpose.
Reflections have determinant -1 and flip orientation; across y = x the matrix swaps x and y.
Shear (x, y) -> (x + k y, y) tilts shapes but keeps area (determinant 1).
To chain moves, multiply matrices with the first move on the right; order matters (FR is not RF).
Translation is not linear, but homogeneous coordinates (x, y, 1) with 3 x 3 matrices make it a matrix product.
Rotation about a point c is T(c) R T(-c); 3D graphics uses 4 x 4 homogeneous matrices.
lessons.tip: For any transformation matrix, test it on (1, 0) and (0, 1) and sketch the results. If the little L-shape they make turns, stretches or flips the way you expect, your matrix is right.
lessons.task: On graph paper, draw the triangle (0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1). Apply a 90 degree rotation, then a reflection across the x-axis, and draw the result. Then apply them in the opposite order and draw again. Confirm the two pictures differ and that the area stays 1 both times.

quiz.q: Which matrix rotates points 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin?
quiz.explain: It must send (1, 0) to (0, 1) and (0, 1) to (-1, 0); those are its columns, giving rows (0, -1) and (1, 0).

quiz.q: What is the determinant of any reflection matrix in 2D?
quiz.explain: Reflections keep area but flip orientation, so the determinant is -1.

quiz.q: Why can no 2 x 2 matrix translate every point by (3, 4)?
options: Any matrix sends (0, 0) to (0, 0), but translation moves the origin
quiz.explain: Linear maps fix the origin; translation moves it to (3, 4), so it needs homogeneous coordinates.

quiz.q: Using homogeneous coordinates, where does the point (2, 3) go under translation by (5, -1)?
A shear (x, y) -> (x + 2y, y) is applied to a shape of area 5. What is the new area?
quiz.explain: The shear matrix has rows (1, 2) and (0, 1), determinant 1, so area is unchanged.

lessons.title: Change of Basis and Similar Matrices
lessons.content:
Imagine you ask two people in Dhaka for directions to the same tea stall. One says: walk 300 metres north and then 400 metres east. The other, who always thinks in terms of the main road that runs at a slant, says: walk 500 metres straight along the main road. Both are describing the very same spot. The tea stall did not move. Only the way of describing it changed. That is the whole idea of this lesson: the same vector, and the same transformation, can be written with different numbers depending on which basis you use to describe them.

Where we are in the course: In the basis and dimension lesson you learned that a basis is a set of vectors that is linearly independent and spans the space, and that every vector has unique coordinates relative to a basis. In the linear transformations lesson you learned that a linear map has a matrix. Today we connect these two ideas. We ask: if I switch from one basis to another, how do the coordinates of a vector change, and how does the matrix of a transformation change? The answers are the transition matrix and similar matrices.

Coordinates, a quick reminder: Let B = {b1, b2} be a basis of R^2. If x = c1 b1 + c2 b2, then the coordinate vector of x relative to B is [x]_B = (c1, c2). The standard basis e1 = (1, 0), e2 = (0, 1) is special because the coordinates of x in it are just the entries of x. Any other basis gives different coordinates for the same arrow, just like the two people giving directions.

The basis matrix: Put the basis vectors of B as columns of a matrix P_B = [b1 b2]. Then the equation x = c1 b1 + c2 b2 is exactly x = P_B [x]_B, because a matrix times a vector is a combination of its columns. Since the columns of P_B form a basis, P_B is square and invertible, so we can go the other way: [x]_B = P_B^-1 x. Read this as: P_B turns B-coordinates into standard coordinates, and P_B^-1 turns standard coordinates into B-coordinates.

A worked example: Let b1 = (1, 1) and b2 = (1, -1). Then P = [1 1; 1 -1]. Its determinant is (1)(-1) - (1)(1) = -2, so by the 2x2 inverse formula P^-1 = (1/-2)[-1 -1; -1 1] = [1/2 1/2; 1/2 -1/2]. Take x = (5, 1). Then [x]_B = P^-1 x = (5/2 + 1/2, 5/2 - 1/2) = (3, 2). Check it: 3(1, 1) + 2(1, -1) = (3 + 2, 3 - 2) = (5, 1). Correct. The point (5, 1) in standard coordinates is the point (3, 2) in B-coordinates.

Changing between two non-standard bases: Often neither basis is the standard one. Suppose B and C are two bases of R^n with basis matrices P_B and P_C. To go from B-coordinates to C-coordinates, first go from B to standard (multiply by P_B), then from standard to C (multiply by P_C^-1). So the transition matrix is P_{C<-B} = P_C^-1 P_B, and [x]_C = P_{C<-B} [x]_B. The little arrow C<-B in the name reminds you which way it goes: it eats B-coordinates and gives back C-coordinates.

Example of a transition matrix: Let B = {(1, 0), (1, 1)} and C = {(1, 1), (0, 1)}. Then P_B = [1 1; 0 1] and P_C = [1 0; 1 1]. The inverse of P_C is [1 0; -1 1] (determinant 1, swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal). So P_{C<-B} = [1 0; -1 1][1 1; 0 1] = [1 1; -1 0]. Test it on [x]_B = (2, 3). The actual vector is 2(1, 0) + 3(1, 1) = (5, 3). The matrix gives [x]_C = (2 + 3, -2 + 0) = (5, -2). Check: 5(1, 1) - 2(0, 1) = (5, 3). It works.

Useful facts about transition matrices: Every transition matrix is invertible, and going back is just its inverse: P_{B<-C} = (P_{C<-B})^-1. Transitions chain together: P_{D<-B} = P_{D<-C} P_{C<-B}. A second way to build P_{C<-B} by hand is to row reduce the big augmented matrix [P_C | P_B] until the left side becomes the identity; the right side is then P_{C<-B}. This is the same trick you used to find inverses with Gauss-Jordan, and it avoids computing P_C^-1 separately.

Now the transformation side: Let T be a linear transformation from R^n to R^n with standard matrix A, so T(x) = Ax. In a basis B, T also has a matrix, written [T]_B. Its job is: take the B-coordinates of x and return the B-coordinates of T(x). We can build it from the trip we already know: start with [x]_B, convert to standard with P, apply A, then convert back with P^-1. So [T]_B = P^-1 A P, where P = P_B. Many textbooks write this as B^-1 A B, using B for the matrix whose columns are the basis vectors.

Column by column view: There is a second way to find [T]_B that is often faster. Its j-th column is the B-coordinate vector of T(bj). So you apply T to each basis vector and ask: how do I write the result in terms of the basis? This is exactly how we built the matrix of a transformation before, except now the answers are recorded in B-coordinates instead of standard coordinates.

A beautiful example: Take A = [3 1; 1 3] and the basis b1 = (1, 1), b2 = (1, -1) from before. Compute A b1 = (3 + 1, 1 + 3) = (4, 4) = 4 b1. Compute A b2 = (3 - 1, 1 - 3) = (2, -2) = 2 b2. So in B-coordinates, T just stretches the first coordinate by 4 and the second by 2. That means [T]_B = [4 0; 0 2], a diagonal matrix. Let us confirm with the formula: AP = [4 2; 4 -2], and P^-1 (AP) = [1/2 1/2; 1/2 -1/2][4 2; 4 -2] = [4 0; 0 2]. Same answer.

Why this is exciting: In the standard basis, A = [3 1; 1 3] looks like it mixes x and y together. In the basis B it is revealed as something very simple: stretch by 4 along the line y = x, and stretch by 2 along the line y = -x. Nothing is mixed. A good basis turned a confusing matrix into a diagonal one. Diagonal matrices are the easiest of all to understand, to multiply and to raise to powers, because you just work on each diagonal entry separately.

Similar matrices: Two square matrices A and C are called similar if there is an invertible matrix P with C = P^-1 A P. Similar matrices are really the same linear transformation seen from two different bases. In our example, A = [3 1; 1 3] and D = [4 0; 0 2] are similar. Similarity is an equivalence relation: every matrix is similar to itself (take P = I), if A is similar to C then C is similar to A (use P^-1), and if A is similar to C and C to E, then A is similar to E (multiply the P's).

What similar matrices share: Because they describe the same transformation, similar matrices agree on everything that does not depend on the choice of basis. They have the same determinant, since det(P^-1 A P) = det(P^-1) det(A) det(P) = det(A). They have the same trace (sum of diagonal entries), the same rank, the same characteristic polynomial and therefore the same eigenvalues. Check our example: trace of A is 3 + 3 = 6 and trace of D is 4 + 2 = 6. Determinant of A is 9 - 1 = 8 and of D is 4 x 2 = 8. Both match.

What they do not share: Similar matrices usually have different entries and different eigenvectors written as columns of numbers, because eigenvectors are coordinates, and coordinates depend on the basis. The underlying arrows are the same, only their descriptions change. Also be careful with the other direction: having the same eigenvalues does not guarantee similarity. The identity I = [1 0; 0 1] and the matrix J = [1 1; 0 1] both have eigenvalues 1 and 1, the same trace 2 and the same determinant 1, yet they are not similar, because P^-1 I P = I for every P, so the only matrix similar to I is I itself.

Why a good basis helps: The whole point of changing basis is to make a problem simpler. If you can find a basis in which your matrix is diagonal, then computing A^100 becomes easy, solving systems of differential equations becomes easy, and understanding the geometry becomes easy. Finding such a basis is exactly what eigenvectors do, and that is the topic of the eigenvalue and diagonalization lessons later in this course. For now, remember the formula A = P D P^-1 as a preview: it is just [T]_B = P^-1 A P solved for A.

A small preview of powers: With A = P D P^-1, A^2 = P D P^-1 P D P^-1 = P D^2 P^-1, because the middle P^-1 P cancels to I. In general A^k = P D^k P^-1, and D^k is just each diagonal entry raised to the k-th power. For our A, D^10 = [4^10 0; 0 2^10] = [1048576 0; 0 1024]. Doing ten full 2x2 multiplications by hand would be slow and error prone; this way it is one easy step plus two multiplications.

Real-life example 1, maps and buildings: An architect in Dhaka draws a building plan with axes along the walls of the plot. But the plot is tilted relative to true north, as many plots along a slanted road are. The city's map uses north and east as its axes. To place the plan on the city map, software multiplies every corner point by a change-of-basis matrix (here a rotation, plus a shift for the origin). The building is the same; only the coordinate system changes. Game engines and 3D graphics do this all the time when they convert between object space, world space and camera space.

Real-life example 2, pictures and sound: When your phone saves a JPEG photo, it does not store each 8x8 block of pixels directly. It changes basis to a set of cosine patterns using the discrete cosine transform (DCT). In the new basis most coordinates are tiny and can be rounded off or thrown away, which is why a photo you share on Facebook or WhatsApp becomes so much smaller. Audio formats like MP3 also use a cosine-type change of basis. The same data, a smarter basis, far fewer numbers to store.

Common mistakes: The most common slip is getting the direction wrong. P_B turns B-coordinates into standard coordinates, and P_B^-1 does the reverse. If you write P A P^-1 when you meant P^-1 A P, you get the matrix in a different basis than the one you wanted. Always test with one vector. A second mistake is forgetting that the basis matrix must be invertible; if your proposed basis vectors are dependent, you do not have a basis at all. A third is thinking that similar means equal; similar matrices usually look very different.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: find [x]_B for a given basis; find the transition matrix from B to C and use it; find the matrix of T relative to a basis B; show that two matrices are similar by finding P; or prove that similar matrices have the same determinant, trace or eigenvalues. A classic trick question asks whether two matrices with different traces or determinants can be similar. The answer is no, and one line of reasoning about invariants is enough.

Recap: A basis is a choice of measuring sticks. The basis matrix P_B converts B-coordinates to standard coordinates, and the transition matrix from B to C is P_C^-1 P_B. A linear transformation with standard matrix A has matrix P^-1 A P in the basis whose vectors are the columns of P. Matrices related this way are similar: they share determinant, trace, rank and eigenvalues. The reason we care is that a clever basis can turn a messy matrix into a diagonal one, which is the road to eigenvalues, diagonalization, PCA and much more.
key_points: If P_B has the basis vectors of B as columns, then x = P_B [x]_B and [x]_B = P_B^-1 x.
The transition matrix from B to C is P_{C<-B} = P_C^-1 P_B; going back uses its inverse.
The matrix of T (standard matrix A) in basis B is [T]_B = P^-1 A P with P = P_B.
Column j of [T]_B is the B-coordinate vector of T(bj).
A and C are similar if C = P^-1 A P for some invertible P: same transformation, different basis.
Similar matrices share determinant, trace, rank, characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues.
Same eigenvalues do not guarantee similarity: I and [1 1; 0 1] are not similar.
A good basis can make a matrix diagonal, which makes powers and geometry easy.
lessons.tip: Every time you write a change-of-basis formula, test it on one simple vector like a basis vector. If P^-1 A P sends b1 to the wrong thing, you have the direction backwards, and you will catch it in ten seconds.
lessons.task: Take A = [2 1; 1 2] and the basis b1 = (1, 1), b2 = (1, -1). Compute A b1 and A b2 by hand and write [T]_B. Then compute P^-1 A P with P = [1 1; 1 -1] and check you get the same diagonal matrix. Finally compare the trace and determinant of A and [T]_B.

quiz.q: If P_B has the vectors of basis B as its columns, which formula gives the B-coordinates of x?
quiz.explain: x = P_B [x]_B, so multiplying both sides by P_B^-1 gives [x]_B = P_B^-1 x. (P_B^T works only when the basis is orthonormal.)

quiz.q: Which expression is the transition matrix from basis B to basis C?
quiz.explain: First go from B to standard with P_B, then from standard to C with P_C^-1, giving P_C^-1 P_B.

quiz.q: A = [3 1; 1 3] and b1 = (1, 1), b2 = (1, -1). What is the matrix of A in this basis?
quiz.explain: A b1 = 4 b1 and A b2 = 2 b2, so the columns of [T]_B are (4, 0) and (0, 2).

quiz.q: Which property is NOT guaranteed to be the same for two similar matrices?
options: The entries in the first row
quiz.explain: Similar matrices share basis-independent quantities like determinant, trace and eigenvalues, but their entries usually differ.

quiz.q: A has trace 5 and C has trace 7. Can A and C be similar?
options: No, similar matrices have equal trace
Only if det A = det C
quiz.explain: Trace is a similarity invariant, so different traces rule out similarity immediately.

lessons.title: Orthogonality, Gram-Schmidt and QR
lessons.content:
Think about the walls and floor in the corner of your room. The two walls and the floor meet at perfect right angles. If you want to say where a fly is sitting, you measure how far it is from each wall and from the floor, and those three numbers never interfere with each other. Moving the fly toward one wall does not change its distance from the floor. Right angles make measuring clean and independent. That cleanness is what orthogonality gives us in linear algebra, and it is why mathematicians and programmers love orthogonal things.

Where we are: In the dot product lesson you learned that two vectors u and v are orthogonal when u . v = 0, and you learned to project one vector onto another. In the basis lessons you learned that a basis gives coordinates. Today we combine these: what happens when every vector in a basis is at right angles to every other? We will meet orthogonal and orthonormal sets, orthogonal matrices, the Gram-Schmidt process that builds such a basis, and the QR factorization that packages the result.

Orthogonal sets: A set of vectors {u1, u2, ..., uk} is called an orthogonal set if every pair of different vectors in it is orthogonal, that is ui . uj = 0 whenever i is not equal to j. For example, u1 = (1, 1, 0), u2 = (1, -1, 2) and u3 = (-1, 1, 1) form an orthogonal set. Check: u1 . u2 = 1 - 1 + 0 = 0, u1 . u3 = -1 + 1 + 0 = 0, and u2 . u3 = -1 - 1 + 2 = 0. All three dot products are zero.

Orthogonal means independent: Here is a lovely fact. Any orthogonal set of nonzero vectors is automatically linearly independent. Why? Suppose c1 u1 + c2 u2 + ... + ck uk = 0. Take the dot product of both sides with u1. Every term except the first dies, because u1 is orthogonal to the others, leaving c1 (u1 . u1) = 0. Since u1 is nonzero, u1 . u1 is positive, so c1 = 0. The same trick with u2, u3 and so on gives every c equal to zero. So an orthogonal set of n nonzero vectors in R^n is always a basis, without any row reduction.

Coordinates the easy way: Normally, to find the coordinates of x in a basis, you must solve a system of equations. With an orthogonal basis you just compute dot products. If x = c1 u1 + ... + cn un, dot both sides with uj to get x . uj = cj (uj . uj), so cj = (x . uj) / (uj . uj). Example: write x = (3, 1, 2) in the basis above. c1 = (3 + 1 + 0)/2 = 2, c2 = (3 - 1 + 4)/6 = 1, c3 = (-3 + 1 + 2)/3 = 0. Check: 2(1, 1, 0) + 1(1, -1, 2) + 0 = (3, 1, 2). Correct, and no elimination needed.

Orthonormal sets: An orthogonal set in which every vector also has length 1 is called orthonormal.
